140: \section{Background}
141: \label{sec:background}
142: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
143: 
144: \subsection{Latent Diffusion for Audio}
145: \label{subsec:bg_lda}
146: 
147: Latent diffusion models~\cite{rombach2022} move the expensive iterative
148: denoising process from pixel (or waveform) space into a compressed
149: continuous latent space produced by a pretrained autoencoder, drastically
150: reducing computation while retaining high-fidelity synthesis.
151: EnCodec~\cite{defossez2022} provides the audio equivalent: a neural codec
152: operating at 24\,kHz that encodes mono audio clips into a 1-D continuous
153: latent $z \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times T}$ (with $D=128$, $T=375$ for 5-second
154: clips) via its pre-quantization continuous features.
155: 
156: \placeholder{Discuss related audio generative models (AudioLM, MusicGen,
157: Stable Audio, AudioCraft). Contrast with symbolic-only (MIDI) and
158: waveform-only generation. Motivate the spectral-latent approach.}
159: 
160: \subsection{ArrowSpace Graph Priors and Energy-Dispersion Networks}
161: \label{subsec:bg_arrowspace}
162: 
163: ArrowSpace~\cite{arrowspace_joss} defines a spectral search framework for
164: embeddings in which feature columns of a corpus feature matrix
165: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times F}$ are treated as nodes of a feature-space
166: graph $G_F = (V_F, W_F)$ with $|V_F|=F$. The feature-space graph
167: Laplacian
168: \begin{equation}
169:   L_F = D^{-1/2}(D - W)D^{-1/2}, \qquad L_F = U\Lambda U^\top,
170:   \label{eq:laplacian}
171: \end{equation}
172: has eigenvectors $U_q \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times q}$ (the $q$ smoothest
173: modes) that define the semantic subspace of the corpus.
174: 
175: The Energy Dispersion Network (EDN)~\cite{edn2025} associates to each
176: feature $f$ a per-feature energy-dispersion scalar
177: $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}_f \in [0,1]$, encoding how semantic structure is
178: distributed over the feature graph. Projected onto the chart, these give
179: per-mode dispersion weights
180: \begin{equation}
181:   \lambda^{\mathrm{chart}}_k
182:   = \sum_{f=1}^{F} \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}_f \, U_{f,k}^2.
183:   \label{eq:chart_dispersion}
184: \end{equation}
185:

187: graph construction, $\tau$-modulation, and the connection between

190: \subsection{Entropic Time Scheduling and the Barontini Clock}
191: \label{subsec:bg_clock}
192: 
193: The entropic (Barontini) clock~\cite{barontini2026,stancevic2025} provides
194: an intrinsic, spectrally-informed stopping criterion for diffusion
195: sampling. Per-mode entropy-time coordinates are defined as
196: \begin{equation}
197:   \tau_k(t) = \nu_k \bar{\alpha}_k(t),
198:   \label{eq:entropic_time}
199: \end{equation}
200: where $\nu_k$ are the eigenvalues of $L_F$ and $\bar{\alpha}_k(t)$ is the
201: mode-$k$ noise schedule. The sampler terminates when
202: \begin{equation}
203:   \sum_{k=1}^{q} \nu_k \, \bar{\alpha}_k(t) < \varepsilon,
204:   \label{eq:heat_death}
205: \end{equation}
206: the ``heat-death'' criterion, replacing an arbitrary fixed step count
207: with a spectrally-motivated halting rule~\cite{lsd,aldsc}.

214: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
215: \section{Spectral Composition}
216: \label{sec:method}
217: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
218: 
219: We now define the four stages of the Spectral Composition pipeline
220: formally. Let $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}$ denote the producer's
221: sound archive (a set of raw audio clips), and let $\mathcal{M}$ denote a
222: trained LSD model (frozen prior + graph decoder + 1-D DiT).
223: 
224: \subsection{Stage 1 — Spectral Encoding (Library Dehydration)}
225: \label{subsec:stage1}
226: 
227: \subsubsection{EnCodec feature extraction}
228: 
229: Each clip $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ is encoded by the frozen EnCodec encoder
230: $E_\phi$ (24\,kHz mono, never updated) to produce:
231: \begin{equation}
232:   (z_i,\; A_i) = E_\phi(x_i),
233:   \qquad
234:   z_i \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times T},\quad
235:   A_i = \mathrm{Pool}(z_i) \in \mathbb{R}^F.
236:   \label{eq:encodec}
237: \end{equation}
238: The pooled feature field $A_i$ is the row contributed by clip $i$ to the
239: corpus feature matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times F}$.
240: 
241: \subsubsection{ArrowSpace prior construction}
242: 
243: From $A$ the ArrowSpace adapter builds the frozen feature-space graph
244: Laplacian $L_F$ and energy-dispersion network $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$
245: via the \texttt{pyarrowspace} library~\cite{pyarrowspace}. The eigenvectors
246: $U_q$ and eigenvalues $\nu_k$ are stored as non-trainable buffers. The
247: spectral conditioning vector for a clip is
248: \begin{equation}
249:   c_{\mathrm{spec}} =
250:   \bigl[\tilde{e},\; \lambda^{\mathrm{chart}},\; \nu\bigr]
251:   \in \mathbb{R}^{3q},
252:   \label{eq:cspec}
253: \end{equation}
254: where $\tilde{e}_k$ is the per-mode band energy. The entire library is
255: now represented by the compact frozen objects
256: $(L_F, U_q, \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}})$ — the \emph{dehydrated} spectral
257: representation.
258: 
259: \subsubsection{Two-stage model training}
260: 
261: Training proceeds as two frozen-then-fine-tuned phases.
262: In Phase 1 the graph decoder is trained with optional latent-space noise
263: injection (parameter \texttt{NOISE\_INJECT} $\in [0, \infty)$).
264: In Phase 2 the 1-D DiT denoiser is trained on the corpus latents
265: $\{z_i\}$ conditioned on $c_{\mathrm{spec}}$:
266: \begin{equation}
267:   \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}
268:   = \mathbb{E}_{z_0,\epsilon,t}
269:     \left\|v - v_\theta(z_t,\, t,\, c_{\mathrm{spec}})\right\|_2^2,
270:   \label{eq:diffusion_loss}
271: \end{equation}
272: using $v$-prediction for numerical stability.
273: 
274: \placeholder{Describe the full training loss including $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$
275: (L1 + multi-scale STFT), $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chart}}$, and
276: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}}$. Discuss the non-repeatable training
277: design (SEED=None, NOISE\_INJECT).}
278: 
279: \subsection{Stage 2 — Dense Unconditional Sampling (Sound-Bank Generation)}
280: \label{subsec:stage2}
281: 
282: Given trained $\mathcal{M}$, a sound bank $\mathcal{B}$ of $n$ clips is
283: generated by running the DDIM or Euler sampler on the 1-D DiT
284: unconditionally, then decoding through the
285: \texttt{ClockGatedGraphDecoder}:
286: \begin{equation}
287:   \hat{z}^{(j)} \sim p_\theta(z \mid c_{\mathrm{spec}}),
288:   \qquad j = 1, \ldots, n,
289:   \label{eq:sampling}
290: \end{equation}
291: \begin{equation}
292:   \hat{x}^{(j)} = D_\psi\!\left(\hat{z}^{(j)};\;
293:     U_q,\; \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}},\; c_{\mathrm{spec}}^{(j)}\right),
294:   \label{eq:decoding}
295: \end{equation}
296: where $c_{\mathrm{spec}}^{(j)}$ is derived \emph{self-consistently} from
297: $\hat{z}^{(j)}$ itself (no separate chart sampling required). The bank
298: $\mathcal{B} = \{\hat{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \hat{x}^{(n)}\}$ consists of
299: samples that are perceptually self-similar — drawn from the same frozen
300: manifold — yet acoustically distinct because \texttt{SEED=None} is the
301: default.
302: 
303: \placeholder{Discuss the ``super-dense'' character of the bank: why
304: all samples share stylistic identity while varying locally. Relate to the
305: frozen prior design constraint (corpus-level prior, not per-clip).}
306: 
307: \subsection{Stage 3 — MIDI-Conditioned Materialisation (Rehydration)}
308: \label{subsec:stage3}
309: 
310: \subsubsection{Language-model MIDI generation}
311: 
312: A language model (e.g.\ a GPT-based symbolic music model) generates a MIDI
313: file $\mathcal{P}$ = $\{(p_i, t_i, d_i)\}$ where $p_i$ is the MIDI pitch,
314: $t_i$ the onset time, and $d_i$ the duration of note $i$.
315: 
316: \placeholder{Describe the GPT-MIDI generation front-end: prompt design,
317: conditioning on genre/key/BPM, and the interface to LSD-Studio. Discuss
318: alternative symbolic sources (human MIDI, rule-based generation, MusicXML).}
319: 
320: \subsubsection{Pitch-shifted decoding (synthesize\_midi)}
321: 
322: For each note $(p_i, t_i, d_i)$ the adapter selects a bank clip
323: $\hat{x}^{(j)}$ and applies pitch-shifting to MIDI pitch $p_i$ via the
324: \texttt{synthesize\_midi} method of \texttt{LSDModel}:
325: \begin{equation}
326:   y_i = \mathrm{PitchShift}\!\left(\hat{x}^{(j)},\;
327:     \Delta p_i\right)\bigg|_{[t_i,\; t_i + d_i]},
328:   \label{eq:pitchshift}
329: \end{equation}
330: where $\Delta p_i$ is the semitone offset from the bank clip's reference
331: pitch. The materialised output is
332: \begin{equation}
333:   Y^{(1)} = \sum_i y_i,
334:   \label{eq:materialise}
335: \end{equation}
336: a waveform that follows the symbolic structure of $\mathcal{P}$ while
337: carrying the spectral identity of the source library.
338: 
339: \subsubsection{Audio-conditioned variant generation}
340: 
341: Optionally, the materialised output $Y^{(1)}$ is fed back into the model
342: via \texttt{condition\_on\_audio} (Mode~B) to generate variants:
343: \begin{equation}
344:   \hat{z}' \sim p_\theta(z \mid z_{\mathrm{cond}} + \eta),
345:   \qquad \eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),
346:   \label{eq:conditioned_sampling}
347: \end{equation}
348: where $z_{\mathrm{cond}} = E_\phi(Y^{(1)})$ is the conditioning latent
349: and $\sigma$ is the perturbation strength. The chart conditioning
350: $c_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is re-derived from $\hat{z}'$, keeping the output on
351: the archive manifold.
352: 
353: \subsection{Stage 4 — Recursive Variant Generation}
354: \label{subsec:stage4}
355: 
356: Stages~2 and~3 are applied recursively. Let $\mathcal{P}^{(1)}, \ldots,
357: \mathcal{P}^{(R)}$ be $R$ distinct MIDI files (generated by the language
358: model or supplied by the producer). The recursive scheme is:
359: \begin{align}
360:   \mathcal{B}^{(0)} &= \texttt{generate\_sound\_bank}(n),
361:   \label{eq:recursive_init}\\
362:   Y^{(r)} &= \texttt{synthesize\_midi}\!\left(\mathcal{P}^{(r)},\;
363:     \mathcal{B}^{(r-1)}\right),
364:   \label{eq:recursive_synth}\\
365:   \mathcal{B}^{(r)} &= \texttt{condition\_on\_audio}\!\left(Y^{(r)},\;
366:     n,\; \sigma_r\right),
367:   \qquad r = 1, \ldots, R.
368:   \label{eq:recursive_cond}
369: \end{align}
370: Each round deepens the stylistic imprint of the source library while
371: incorporating new symbolic content from $\mathcal{P}^{(r)}$. The family
372: $\{Y^{(1)}, \ldots, Y^{(R)}\}$ constitutes a set of \emph{variants}
373: related by shared spectral ancestry.
374: 
375: \subsubsection{Convergence and heat-death stopping}
376: 
377: The recursive process is bounded intrinsically by the heat-death criterion
378: (Eq.~\ref{eq:heat_death}): if the conditioning latent $z_{\mathrm{cond}}$
379: has collapsed to a near-constant spectral chart, additional conditioning
380: passes yield diminishing novelty. In practice, the producer controls depth
381: via $R$ and the perturbation schedule $\{\sigma_r\}$.
382: 
383: \subsection{Final Assembly — Multitrack Mixing}
384: \label{subsec:mixing}
385: 
386: The variant outputs $\{Y^{(1)}, \ldots, Y^{(R)}\}$ plus any selections
387: from the unconditional bank $\mathcal{B}^{(0)}$ form a natural stem set
388: for a multitrack mix. Within LSD-Studio, these are routed to a mix bus
389: with per-stem gain, panning, and effect chains. Additional post-processing
390: (overlap-and-add long-form generation, BPS-synchronised modulation,
391: latent-space concatenation) is available via the notebook series
392: (02--04)~\cite{lsd}.
393:

399: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
400: \section{System Architecture}
401: \label{sec:architecture}
402: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
403: 
404: \subsection{Frozen ArrowSpace Prior and Manifold Construction}
405: \label{subsec:arch_prior}
406: 
407: The ArrowSpace prior is built once from the corpus by \texttt{build\_prior.py}
408: and stored as non-trainable buffers:
409: \begin{equation}
410:   \Pi_q = U_q U_q^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times F},
411:   \label{eq:projector}
412: \end{equation}
413: the spectral projector onto the smooth subspace. The frozen design
414: constraint means that $L_F$ and $U_q$ never receive gradient updates;
415: only the graph decoder and DiT are trained. This ensures that the
416: manifold geometry is a property of the \emph{corpus}, not a function of
417: any single training run.
418: 
419: \placeholder{Describe the kNN graph construction, the ArrowSpace library
420: API (\texttt{gl}, \texttt{lambdas()}), and the fallback behaviour when
421: \texttt{pyarrowspace} bindings are unavailable.}
422: 
423: \subsection{1-D DiT Denoiser}
424: \label{subsec:arch_dit}
425: 
426: The denoiser \texttt{MinimalDiT} patchifies the 1-D latent
427: $z \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times T}$ with stride-$s$ convolutions, applies
428: $L$ transformer blocks with AdaLN conditioning on $(t, c_{\mathrm{spec}})$,
429: and unpatchifies to predict velocity $v$. Classifier-free guidance (CFG)
430: is applied by randomly dropping $c_{\mathrm{spec}}$ during training with
431: probability $p_{\mathrm{drop}}$, enabling guidance-scale control at
432: inference.
433: 
434: \subsection{Graph Decoder}
435: \label{subsec:arch_decoder}
436: 
437: The \texttt{ClockGatedGraphDecoder} processes the denoised latent
438: $\hat{z}$ through a sequence of \texttt{WaveReconstructionBlock}s:
439: \begin{align}
440:   \hat{H} &= A \cdot U_q,
441:   \label{eq:project_chart}\\
442:   g &= \sigma(W_g \cdot c_{\mathrm{spec}})\; \odot\; \bar{\alpha}(t),
443:   \label{eq:gate}\\
444:   A' &= (\hat{H} \odot g) \cdot U_q^\top + A_{\mathrm{res}},
445:   \label{eq:lift}
446: \end{align}
447: where $A_{\mathrm{res}}$ is a residual convolution path and
448: $\bar{\alpha}(t)$ is the Barontini clock gate (weak early in denoising,
449: strong late). The decoder thus allocates reconstruction energy according
450: to the corpus dispersion $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$, not arbitrary learned
451: weights.
452: 
453: \subsection{Inference Contract (A / B / C)}
454: \label{subsec:arch_inference}
455: 
456: \texttt{LSDModel} (defined in \texttt{src/ald\_sc/inference.py})
457: exposes three methods that directly implement Stages~2--4:
458: 
459: \begin{description}
460:   \item[Mode A: \texttt{generate\_sound\_bank(n, steps, temperature, seed)}]
461:     Unconditional DiT sampling + graph decode. Implements Stage~2.
462:   \item[Mode B: \texttt{condition\_on\_audio(audio, n, strength, seed)}]
463:     Conditioned sampling with SDE bridge toward the input latent.
464:     Used in Stage~4 feedback loops.
465:   \item[Mode C: \texttt{synthesize\_midi(midi\_path, bank, seed)}]
466:     Pitch-shifted bank decoding driven by a MIDI file.
467:     Implements Stage~3.
468: \end{description}
469:

471: \label{subsec:arch_studio}
472: 
473: LSD-Studio~\cite{lsdstudio} is a Rust + \texttt{iced} desktop
474: application that wraps the Python LSD model workers and exposes the
475: full Spectral Composition workflow to the producer: library ingestion,
476: model baking, sound-bank auditioning, MIDI sequencing, recursive

488: 
489: \subsection{Software Stack}
490: \label{subsec:impl_stack}
491: 
492: The LSD model core is implemented in Python~3.13 with PyTorch~$\geq$2.2,
493: using \texttt{uv} for dependency management. The graph prior is computed
494: via \texttt{pyarrowspace} (Rust bindings). LSD-Studio is implemented in
495: Rust (stable) with the \texttt{iced} GUI framework and communicates with
496: Python workers over a JSON-RPC IPC channel. The full source code,
497: evaluation pipeline, and trained-model checkpoints are available at
498: \url{https://github.com/tuned-org-uk/latent-sound-diffusion}.

523: \subsection{Training Details}

1: """Build the frozen ArrowSpace prior from corpus embeddings.
2: 
3: Constructs the feature-space graph Laplacian via kNN over feature columns
4: (the ArrowSpace dual-space construction), eigendecomposes it, and returns
5: an ``ArrowSpacePrior`` with frozen buffers.
6: 
7: This module must not import ``torch.nn`` modules (per AGENTS.md §11).
8: """
9: 
10: from __future__ import annotations
11: 
12: import torch
13: from torch import Tensor
14: 
15: from ald_sc.arrow_prior import ArrowSpacePrior
16: 
17: __all__ = ["build_arrow_prior", "build_feature_laplacian", "build_projector"]
18: 
19: 
20: def build_feature_laplacian(embeddings: Tensor, k: int = 8) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
21:     """Build the feature-space graph Laplacian from a corpus of embeddings.
22: 
23:     Features are columns of the embedding matrix. The kNN graph is built on
24:     cosine similarity between feature signals (columns), exactly as in
25:     ArrowSpace's feature-Laplacian construction.
26: 
27:     Parameters
28:     ----------
29:     embeddings : Tensor (N, F)
30:         Corpus of N embeddings with F features each.
31:     k : int
32:         Number of nearest neighbours per feature.
33: 
34:     Returns
35:     -------
36:     L_F : Tensor (F, F)
37:         Unnormalised feature-space Laplacian (D - W).
38:     W : Tensor (F, F)
39:         Symmetrised adjacency matrix.
40:     """
41:     X = embeddings.detach().float()
42:     N, F = X.shape
43: 
44:     X_feat = X.T
45:     norms = X_feat.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-12)
46:     X_norm = X_feat / norms
47:     S = X_norm @ X_norm.T
48: 
49:     W = torch.zeros_like(S)
50:     for i in range(F):
51:         nbrs = torch.argsort(-S[i])[1 : k + 1]
52:         W[i, nbrs] = S[i, nbrs]
53:     W = torch.maximum(W, W.T)
54: 
55:     D = torch.diag(W.sum(dim=1))
56:     L = D - W
57:     return L, W
58: 
59: 
60: def build_projector(
61:     L_F: Tensor, q: int, drop_constant: bool = True
62: ) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
63:     """Compute the leading q eigenvectors of the Laplacian.
64: 
65:     Parameters
66:     ----------
67:     L_F : Tensor (F, F)
68:         Feature-space Laplacian.
69:     q : int
70:         Number of smooth modes to retain.
71:     drop_constant : bool
72:         If True, skip the first (trivial constant) eigenvector.
73: 
74:     Returns
75:     -------
76:     U_q : Tensor (F, q)
77:         Leading q eigenvectors.
78:     eigvals_q : Tensor (q,)
79:         Corresponding eigenvalues.
80:     """
81:     eigvals, eigvecs = torch.linalg.eigh(L_F)
82:     idx = torch.argsort(eigvals)
83:     eigvals = eigvals[idx]
84:     eigvecs = eigvecs[:, idx]
85: 
86:     start = 1 if drop_constant else 0
87:     q = min(q, eigvecs.shape[1] - start)
88:     U_q = eigvecs[:, start : start + q]
89:     eigvals_q = eigvals[start : start + q]
90:     return U_q, eigvals_q
91: 
92: 
93: def _energy_dispersion(embeddings: Tensor) -> Tensor:
94:     """Compute the ArrowSpace energy-dispersion distribution per feature.
95: 
96:     Normalised per-feature energy relative to the total.
97: 
98:     Parameters
99:     ----------
100:     embeddings : Tensor (N, F)
101: 
102:     Returns
103:     -------
104:     Tensor (F,) in [0, 1]
105:     """
106:     X = embeddings.detach().float()
107:     energy = X.pow(2).sum(dim=0)
108:     total = energy.sum() + 1e-12
109:     return energy / total
110: 
111: 
112: def build_arrow_prior(
113:     embeddings: Tensor,
114:     q: int = 16,
115:     k: int = 8,
116: ) -> ArrowSpacePrior:
117:     """Build a frozen ArrowSpacePrior from corpus embeddings.
118: 
119:     Parameters
120:     ----------
121:     embeddings : Tensor (N, F)
122:         Corpus of N embeddings with F features.
123:     q : int
124:         Number of smooth spectral modes to retain.
125:     k : int
126:         kNN neighbours per feature for graph construction.
127: 
128:     Returns
129:     -------
130:     ArrowSpacePrior
131:         Frozen prior with buffers (no trainable parameters).
132:     """
133:     L_F, _ = build_feature_laplacian(embeddings, k=k)
134:     U_q, eigvals_q = build_projector(L_F, q=q)
135:     lambdas_ed = _energy_dispersion(embeddings)
136:     return ArrowSpacePrior(L_F=L_F, U_q=U_q, eigvals_q=eigvals_q, lambdas_ed=lambdas_ed)

input.newString:
Beyond this codec-in-latent-space pattern, the field has explored three
complementary strategies. \emph{Discrete-token language models} —
Jukebox~\cite{jukebox2020}, AudioLM~\cite{audiolm2022}, MusicLM/
MusicGen~\cite{musiclm2023,audiocraft2023} — cast generation as
next-token prediction over neural codec codes, inheriting the long-range
coherence of sequence models but at heavy sampling cost and with identity
tied to massive generic corpora rather than to a producer's own archive.
\emph{Continuous latent diffusion} — Riffusion~\cite{riffusion2022},
AudioLDM~2~\cite{audioldm2_2023}, Stable Audio~\cite{stableaudio2023},
Mo\^usai~\cite{mousai2023} — denoises in a compressed continuous latent
(our setting), trading the discrete hierarchy for sample efficiency and
smooth interpolation; these systems are text-conditioned and corpus-wide,
designed to synthesise arbitrary described audio. \emph{Symbolic
generative models} produce MIDI or scores directly and remain trivially
controllable but carry no timbral identity of their own.

Spectral Composition occupies a deliberately different position. All of
the above condition generation on a \emph{prompt} and evaluate against a
\emph{generic} distribution; none treats a private sound archive as the
primary generative substrate. Our latents come from the producer's
library via a frozen EnCodec encoder~\cite{defossez2022}; our conditioning
vector $c_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is corpus-derived, not text-derived; and our
generation contract (sample, rehydrate, recurse) is a compositional
workflow rather than a single-conditioning synthesis call. Symbolic
structure enters not as the output but as a \emph{control surface}
(Stage~3), combining the controllability of the MIDI world with the
timbral lineage of the latent-diffusion world.

content.text: §2.2 ArrowSpace expansion:

input.newString:
In ArrowSpace's dual-space construction the corpus is viewed through two
graphs: an \emph{item graph} over the $N$ clips and a \emph{feature graph}
over the $F$ feature dimensions, where each feature is represented by its
signal across the corpus (the corresponding column of $A$). Edges of the
feature graph are $k$-nearest-neighbour links under cosine similarity,
symmetrised to keep $L_F$ well-defined. The spectral theorem then
orders features by \emph{smoothness}: the leading eigenvectors $U_q$
span the subspace along which corpus energy varies most coherently —
empirically the directions that encode style and timbral family rather
than idiosyncratic detail. This is the property the ArrowSpace index
exploits at query time via $\lambda\tau$-modulation, weighting chart
coordinates by dispersion to rank spectrally-near neighbours.

The Energy Dispersion Network completes the picture by diagnosing
\emph{how concentrated} the semantic structure of a corpus is:
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}_f$ large on a tightly-connected neighbourhood of
the feature graph means the corpus's meaning is carried by a compact,
redundant feature set — the regime in which aggressive compression (small
$q$) preserves retrieval behaviour. The connection we draw on in this
paper is direct: $\lambda^{\mathrm{chart}}_k$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:chart_dispersion})
measures how much corpus-level dispersion each smooth mode carries, and
we use it to gate how much reconstruction energy the decoder allocates to
that mode. Semantic coherence under compression is thus not an
after-the-fact evaluation but a structural input to decoding.

content.text: §2.3 problem of time (porting the Connes–Rovelli framing from the old paper):

input.newString:
The physical motivation is the \emph{problem of time} in closed systems.
Connes and Rovelli~\cite{connesrovelli1994} argue that in a generally
covariant theory the physical time-flow need not be a universal external
parameter but can arise from the thermodynamical state of the system
itself. Barontini's cold-atom experiment~\cite{barontini2026} provides an
operational testbed: a closed system partitioned into observed and
unobserved sectors admits an \emph{entropic time} constructed purely from
internal entropy exchange between the sectors, without any external
clock. The heat-death criterion above is the sampling-time analogue: the
sampler's progress is measured by how much spectral structure remains
unresolved (internal state), and halting is a property of the trajectory,
not of a step counter.

Among adaptive-sampling methods, DDIM~\cite{song2020} and
DPM-Solver~\cite{lu2022} accelerate diffusion by reusing or integrating
the same fixed schedule more efficiently — the clock is external and
trajectory-independent. The entropic stopping rule is complementary
rather than competing: it says \emph{when individual modes have nothing
left to resolve}, per-mode, driven by the corpus eigenvalues $\nu_k$. In
our implementation the criterion is evaluated as the remaining
dissipation $\sum_k \nu_k (1 - \bar{\alpha}_k(t)) < \varepsilon$, which
decreases monotonically as denoising completes
(Section~\ref{subsec:eval_ablation} measures the resulting
steps-vs-quality tradeoff). We retain this as a design principle —
generative dynamics informed by state-derived geometry — while
acknowledging that the full thermodynamic construction remains a
metaphor-level grounding at this stage.

content.text: §3 training loss (from `losses.py`, with honest disclosure of the current trainer's effective gradient path):

input.newString:
The full training objective for Phase~1 combines four terms:
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{L}
  = \lambda_{\mathrm{rec}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}
  + \lambda_{\mathrm{stft}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stft}}
  + \lambda_{\mathrm{chart}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chart}}
  + \lambda_{\mathrm{smooth}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}},
  \label{eq:total_loss}
\end{equation}
with $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ the waveform L1 distance,
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stft}}$ a multi-scale spectral loss (spectral
convergence + log-magnitude L1 over FFT sizes 512/1024/2048),
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chart}} = \lVert \tilde{e}(A) -
\tilde{e}(\hat{A})\rVert^2$ the spectral-chart consistency between the
band energies of encoder features and their reconstruction, and
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}} = \lVert A (I - U_q U_q^\top)
\rVert_F^2 / \lVert A \rVert_F^2$ the off-manifold penalty. Two
implementation facts matter for interpreting our results, and we state
them plainly. First, in the configuration evaluated in
Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} we set
$\lambda_{\mathrm{stft}} = 0$, so decoder training is driven by the L1
term (with $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chart}}, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}}$
logged as corpus-level diagnostics; in the current trainer the chart
target is detached, so they contribute no decoder gradient). Second, the
chart term as specified — comparing decoded audio re-encoded to
$\hat{A}$ against $A$ — is the natural form of the objective and is
measured as such at evaluation time (Table~\ref{tab:retention}); wiring
it into the decoder gradient is scheduled future work.

The \emph{non-repeatable training} design is deliberate. With
\texttt{SEED=None} a fresh seed is drawn per run, so every baked model —
and therefore every bank and variant family — is a singular artefact:
two producers dehydrating the same library obtain different-but-
lineage-identical manifolds. \texttt{NOISE\_INJECT} ($\sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}$)
perturbs the latent the decoder sees during training (the conditioning
$c_{\mathrm{spec}}$ stays derived from the clean features), trading
reconstruction fidelity for acoustic variety
(Section~\ref{subsec:eval_ablation} quantifies the tradeoff). Training
uses Adam with global gradient-norm clipping at $1.0$; a non-finite
loss or gradient norm aborts the run with an explicit error, a
hardening added after diagnosing an early gradient pathology in the
wave block (Section~\ref{subsec:arch_decoder}).

content.text: §3.2 super-dense bank:

input.newString:
The bank is \emph{super-dense} in the sense that every draw lands on the
same frozen manifold yet no two draws coincide. Three mechanisms
conspire. (i)~The prior is corpus-level, not per-clip: $U_q$ and
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ encode what the \emph{whole library} has in
common — its spectral signature — so every decoded clip is filtered
through the same stylistic identity. (ii)~The unconditional DiT is
trained on latents of the library only; its stationary distribution is
the library's latent distribution, so dense sampling sweeps that
distribution rather than an open-ended audio space. (iii)~The
self-consistent chart conditioning keeps each draw within the energy
allocation the corpus actually exhibits. Locally, draws differ because
the DiT's stationary measure is continuous and
\texttt{SEED=None} makes the sampling trajectory fresh each time;
globally, they agree because every path through Stage~2 crosses the same
projector $\Pi_q$. In producer terms: one bank, many voices, one sound.
This is precisely the behaviour a sample-library workflow wants — a
coherent palette rather than a bag of unrelated one-shots — and it is a
structural consequence of the frozen-prior design, not a tuned
temperature.

content.text: §3.3.1 GPT-MIDI front-end (design spec, honestly framed as not yet built):

input.newString:
\emph{Design specification (not yet implemented).} The front-end is
planned as a small GPT-style decoder over a MIDI event vocabulary
(pitch, onset, duration, velocity), fine-tunable on the producer's own
MIDI corpus so that generated scores match the producer's rhythmic and
harmonic habits. The prompt interface exposes genre, key, and BPM as
structured controls, with a free-text slot for optional style steering;
the model emits a quantised event list validated against the same
$(p_i, t_i, d_i)$ schema that \texttt{synthesize\_midi} consumes, plus
score metadata (BPM, key, time signature) that LSD-Studio propagates to
the transport clock. This component is deliberately swappable: any
source of symbolic material — hand-played MIDI, rule-based generators,
imported MusicXML rendered to MIDI, or clip detection from the archive
itself — feeds Stage~3 unchanged, because the materialisation interface
is the event list, not the language model. In the current system all
MIDI material is supplied manually; the evaluation in
Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} uses fixed scores for exactly this reason
(reproducibility). We report this as an engineering gap, not a
scientific one: nothing in Stages 2--4 depends on how the score was
produced.

content.text: §3.5 DAW integration:

input.newString:
LSD-Studio's mixing surface follows DAW conventions so the workflow
drops into existing practice. Each variant $Y^{(r)}$ and bank selection
occupies a track with the usual gain, pan, mute/solo, and insert chain;
stems created at different recursion depths are grouped, so the variant
family $Y^{(1..R)}$ can be balanced as a unit against the dry bank
$\mathcal{B}^{(0)}$. MIDI synchronisation is planned at the transport
level: the score metadata (BPM, key) emitted by the Stage-3 front-end
sets the project tempo map, note events align to the transport clock,
and re-renders triggered by MIDI edits inherit the running tempo —
materialisation becomes a live, re-renderable instrument rather than a
one-shot bounce. Standard bridge protocols (e.g.\ MIDI-over-IPC to a
DAW, or drag-out of stems) define the boundary with the producer's
existing environment; LSD-Studio does not attempt to replace the DAW
but to sit before it in the pipeline, exporting stems and MIDI. As with
the language-model front-end, this describes the target design: the
current application implements ingestion, baking, auditioning,
generation, and mix-bus routing, with transport-locked re-rendering
scheduled next.

input.newString:
Concretely, \texttt{build\_prior.py} constructs the graph as follows.
Feature signals (columns of the corpus matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N
\times F}$, $F{=}128$ for EnCodec features) are $\ell_2$-normalised and
compared by cosine similarity; each feature is linked to its $k$ nearest
neighbours ($k{=}4$ in the reported configuration), and the adjacency is
symmetrised as $W = \max(W, W^\top)$ so the Laplacian is well-defined.
The unnormalised Laplacian $L_F = D - W$ is eigendecomposed once
(\texttt{torch.linalg.eigh}), eigenvalues sorted ascending, the trivial
constant mode dropped, and the leading $q$ eigenvectors retained as
$U_q$. The dispersion network is the normalised per-feature energy
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}_f = \lVert A_{\cdot f} \rVert_2^2 /
\lVert A \rVert_F^2$, projected onto the chart to yield
$\lambda^{\mathrm{chart}}$. All five objects are frozen buffers with
zero trainable parameters.

The \texttt{wire\_graph.py} adapter is the port to the full ArrowSpace
library: when the \texttt{pyarrowspace} Rust bindings are importable
(exposing the graph constructor \texttt{gl} and dispersion query
\texttt{lambdas()}), $L_F$ and $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ are computed by
the library — the single source of truth, including its sparse
Laplacian normalisation — and the Python kNN construction above serves
as the \emph{fallback} used when the bindings are unavailable (CI,
platforms without the Rust toolchain). The evaluation reported here ran
the fallback path; the two constructions agree on ordering of the
leading modes, and the fallback's dense $128\times128$ Laplacian is
negligible compute at this scale. For archives where $F$ grows with the
feature extractor, the library's sparse implementation is the intended
path (Section~\ref{subsec:eval_limitations}).

content.text: §4.3 describes the old pooled wave block — updating to the v2 per-time-step graph filter (referenced by the training-loss section):

input.newString:
The \texttt{ClockGatedGraphDecoder} processes the denoised latent
$\hat{z}$ through a sequence of \texttt{WaveReconstructionBlock}s, each
applying a \emph{per-time-step graph filter} over the activation field.
With activations $H \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times T}$ and feature projections
$A = W_{C\!\to\!F} H \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times T}$:
\begin{align}
  \hat{H} &= U_q^\top A \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times T},
  \label{eq:project_chart}\\
  g &= \sigma\!\bigl(W_g \, c_{\mathrm{spec}}\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^{q},
  \label{eq:gate}\\
  A' &= U_q \bigl(\hat{H} \odot g \mathbf{1}^\top\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times T},
  \label{eq:lift}
\end{align}
followed by $H' = H + W_{F\!\to\!C} A'$ and a residual
\texttt{GroupNorm--SiLU--Conv1d} block. The gate $g$ is clip-level
(broadcast over time), while the chart round-trip $U_q U_q^\top A$ acts
on every time step independently: each frame is filtered through the
corpus's smooth subspace before reconstruction. The
\texttt{ClockGated} variant additionally modulates the block's
contribution by the Barontini clock $\bar{\alpha}(t)$ — weak early in
denoising, strong late — so the decoder allocates reconstruction energy
according to the corpus dispersion $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ and the
sampling clock, not arbitrary learned weights alone.

An earlier version of this block projected the temporal \emph{mean} of
$H$ through the chart and broadcast the result as a time-constant
per-channel shift before the group normalisation. GroupNorm is
shift-invariant in the forward pass, so that constant's gradient was
carried entirely by second-order terms of the normaliser — a knife-edge
that made early-training stability depend on the noise stream, and
which we diagnosed as the cause of a device-dependent divergence
(loss $0.44 \to 17.8$ on one backend's RNG stream versus stable descent
on another's, at identical seeds and data). The per-time-step
formulation removes the pathology by construction (there is no
time-constant path into the normaliser); gradient clipping and a
non-finite guard in the trainer bound any residual risk. This
experience is reported in detail in the repository's issue
tracker because it is exactly the kind of numerical accident that a
reimplementation of the architecture should be spared.
input.oldString:
The \texttt{ClockGatedGraphDecoder} processes the denoised latent
$\hat{z}$ through a sequence of \texttt{WaveReconstructionBlock}s:
\begin{align}
  \hat{H} &= A \cdot U_q,
  \label{eq:project_chart}\\
  g &= \sigma(W_g \cdot c_{\mathrm{spec}})\; \odot\; \bar{\alpha}(t),
  \label{eq:gate}\\
  A' &= (\hat{H} \odot g) \cdot U_q^\top + A_{\mathrm{res}},
  \label{eq:lift}
\end{align}
where $A_{\mathrm{res}}$ is a residual convolution path and
$\bar{\alpha}(t)$ is the Barontini clock gate (weak early in denoising,
strong late). The decoder thus allocates reconstruction energy according
to the corpus dispersion $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$, not arbitrary learned
weights.

\subsection{Perceptual Coherence of Recursive Variants}
\label{subsec:eval_recursive}

We evaluate the recursion of Stage~4 directly: a fixed three-note score
is rendered from a freshly generated bank (round $0$), and each
subsequent round conditions a new bank on the previous round's render
(\texttt{condition\_on\_audio}, strength $0.5$) and re-renders the same

varied the MIDI content across ``depths''; the measurement here isolates
\emph{recursive feeding itself}. Two independent traces are reported on
the NSynth subset: the CLAP-proxy cosine distance of round $r$'s render
to the round-$0$ render (cumulative novelty), and the spectral
centroid/rolloff drift of the renders.

\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{figures/fig_variant_diversity.png}
\caption{Recursive variant drift over rounds: cumulative novelty
(CLAP-proxy distance to the round-0 render, left) and spectral character
(centroid/rolloff, right). The drift-then-saturate profile matches the
heat-death intuition of Section~\ref{subsec:stage4}.}
\label{fig:recursion}
\end{figure}

The profile is \emph{drift-then-saturate}: novelty jumps in the first
recursion ($0 \to 0.079$), continues to accumulate through round~3
($0.095$), and relaxes slightly at round~4 ($0.081$), while the
spectral centroid rises $606 \to 1536$\,Hz and the rolloff $12 \to
584$\,Hz before plateauing. Qualitatively the same behaviour appears on
ESC-50 (drift to $0.123$, centroid $270 \to 1551$\,Hz): recursion moves
the renders away from the initial draw — locally novel, audibly
brighter — but the family remains anchored, never diverging into
unrelated material. This is the signature the workflow claims: each
round deepens the stylistic imprint while incorporating the score's
structure, with saturation emerging intrinsically rather than being
enforced.

\paragraph{Proposed listening study}
The CLAP-proxy is a distributional check, not a perceptual verdict; we
therefore specify (but have not yet run) the human study that would
substantiate the claim. Design: $20$ producers, $5$ source libraries,

library excerpt and two renders (round $r$ vs.\ a decoy drawn from an
unrelated library), and rates (i)~same-family confidence on a 7-point
scale, (ii)~preference over the round-0 render. Analysis: within-round
family-identification accuracy vs.\ chance (one-sided binomial), and
rating trajectory vs.\ $r$ (Page's trend test). Preregistration,
stimulus generation scripts, and the analysis notebook ship with the
repository so the study can be executed unmodified.

were trained to minimise (L1), the graph decoder edges the baseline on
\emph{every split of both corpora} — margins are small ($3$–$5\%$) and
we make no significance claim at $N{=}256$, but the direction is
consistent, and it is worth noting this comparison flipped in the
graph decoder's favour only after the per-time-step reformulation of
the wave block (the earlier pooled version lost the same comparison
$0.117$ vs $0.114$). Second, on the multi-scale STFT diagnostic — which
neither decoder trained against — the baseline is consistently lower;
the graph decoder spends capacity honouring the chart, which costs it
the spectral-loss metric while winning the waveform metric. Third,
per-band retention (Table~\ref{tab:retention} methodology: re-encode
the reconstruction, compare normalised band energies
$\tilde{e}_k$ against the original's) favours the graph decoder on both
corpora (test cosine $0.998$ vs $0.997$ NSynth; $0.9991$ vs $0.9984$
ESC-50) — the property its architecture is explicitly constrained to
preserve.

\paragraph{Perceptual proxies, stated honestly}
Because \texttt{fadtk} and \texttt{laion-clap} were removed from the
dependency set (conflicts documented in the repository), the
Fr\'echet Audio Distance~\cite{kilgour2019fad} and
CLAP~\cite{laionclap2023} columns are \emph{proxies} computed on the
same frozen EnCodec feature space the model uses: FAD-proxy = Fr\'echet
distance between generated-bank and held-out-test feature distributions
(exact Fr\'echet formula, VGGish embeddings replaced by EnCodec
pooled features); CLAP-proxy = cosine between the bank's mean feature
and a deterministic hashing embedding of the prompt (a stability check,
not a semantics model). On these proxies the baseline is clearly ahead
(NSynth FAD-proxy $408$ vs $1198$; ESC-50 $307$ vs $1787$; CLAP-proxy
$-0.073/-0.065$ vs $-0.046/-0.042$), and we report that gap without
defence. We hypothesise — and this is the experiment the scale-up
should run first — that the gap tracks training scale rather than
architecture: at $20$ epochs on $179$ clips the graph decoder's chart
constraint is a regulariser on an under-trained system, and its
generative distribution has not yet concentrated on the corpus
manifold; the same constraint should pay off as $N$, epochs, and
capacity grow, precisely the regime where unconstrained decoders drift
off-manifold. The compression result
(Table~\ref{tab:compression}), the retention win, and the L1
consistency are the preliminary evidence for that hypothesis; the
FAD-proxy gap is the evidence against, and both are on the table.

content.text: §6.3 ablations (CFG deferred per the confirmed choice):

input.newString:
\subsection{Ablation Studies}
\label{subsec:eval_ablation}

Four ablations, each reported with its honest reading.

\paragraph{$\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ gating (c$_{\mathrm{spec}}$ on/off)}
Zeroing the spectral conditioning at evaluation changes test L1 by
$-2.7\times10^{-5}$ (val $-8.8\times10^{-5}$; train $+8.6\times10^{-4}$):
at this scale the gate is a \textbf{no-op}. This is consistent with the
repository's postmortem of an earlier conditioning regression, and we do
not dress it up — the dispersion-gating mechanism is currently carried
by the architecture, not by an observable training signal. Whether the
gate becomes load-bearing at scale (more modes, longer training) is an
open question the scale-up must answer.

\paragraph{Recursion depth $R$}
Isolated in Section~\ref{subsec:eval_recursive}
(Table~\ref{tab:recursion}): drift-then-saturate, with novelty peaking
at $R{=}3$ ($0.095$) and relaxing at $R{=}4$ ($0.081$).

\paragraph{Chart rank $q$}
Retraining the graph decoder per $q \in \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$ (prior rebuilt
each time) leaves test L1 nearly flat: $0.110, 0.111, 0.114, 0.109$
respectively. Reconstruction at this corpus size is \textbf{not
chart-limited} — consistent with the retention table (mode~0 alone
carries $82\%$ of band energy on NSynth): four smooth modes already
span the energy of this corpus. We expect $q$ to matter only for
corpora with genuinely heterogeneous spectra (ESC-50 is the more
likely candidate; its prior eigenvalue spread is wider).

\paragraph{NOISE\_INJECT $\sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}$}
The diversity-vs-fidelity dial, measured as test L1 against variant
distance (CLAP-proxy pairwise distance among four conditioned variants
of a held-out clip):
$0.0 \to (0.112,\ 6.8{\times}10^{-5})$;
$0.1 \to (0.113,\ 2.4{\times}10^{-4})$;
$0.25 \to (0.109,\ 7.7{\times}10^{-5})$;
$0.5 \to (0.121,\ 1.6{\times}10^{-4})$.
Fidelity degrades monotonically above $\sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}{=}0.25$, but
\textbf{diversity does not track the dial monotonically} at this scale —
the variant distance is dominated by the DDIM noise draw rather than by
the decoder's noise exposure. The dial works as an artistic control
(each setting audibly changes the bank's character); as a measurable
diversity control it is currently weak, and we say so.

\paragraph{Heat-death threshold $\varepsilon$}
Sampling-only, against the corpus scale $\sum_k \nu_k = 5.67$:
$\varepsilon = 0.1$ uses $46$ of $50$ steps (FAD-proxy $1154$);
$0.5 \to 41$ steps ($858$); $1.0 \to 37$ ($883$); $2.0 \to 30$ ($955$);
$5.0 \to 12$ ($1180$). Intrinsic stopping cuts compute $1.2$--$4\times$
\emph{and improves the FAD-proxy in the mid range} — early stopping acts
as implicit truncation of under-resolved high modes, consistent with
the entropic-clock reading. Note the threshold is meaningful only in
absolute units of $\sum\nu$: the first sweep we ran at
$\varepsilon \in \{10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4}\}$ never fired on the
$50$-step grid, a unit error the CSV records.

Classifier-free guidance is absent from this list by decision: the DiT
in the reported configuration is unconditional (time-only AdaLN), so
there is no guidance scale to ablate; text/CLAP conditioning with CFG
is Phase-2 work (Section~\ref{sec:futurework}).

content.text: §6.4 limitations:

input.newString:
The limitations below are concrete and none is fatal to the paradigm;
each names the next measurement.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Proxy metrics.} FAD and CLAP are approximated on EnCodec
    features (Section~\ref{subsec:eval_reconstruction}). The proxies are
    faithful in form but not anchored to VGGish/CLAP semantics; any
    finding within a factor of $\sim$2 of a comparison should be treated
    as unresolved until the original metrics are restored.
  \item \textbf{Preliminary scale.} Every number comes from $256$ clips,
    $20$ epochs, $179$ training samples, $32$ base channels. The L1 win
    and the FAD-proxy gap are both within the range that training noise
    at this scale can produce; the paper's claims are calibrated
    accordingly (and the sweep/retraining infrastructure exists to
    re-run everything at the next scale).
  \item \textbf{Idle gating.} The $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ gate is a no-op
    at this scale (Section~\ref{subsec:eval_ablation}); the chart
    constraint influences decoding through $U_q$ alone.
  \item \textbf{Training instability history.} The original pooled wave
    block diverged stochastically (loss $0.76 \to 11.1$ in the first
    observation) depending on the RNG stream; the per-time-step
    reformulation, gradient clipping, and a non-finite guard (described
    in Section~\ref{subsec:arch_decoder}) removed the pathology, and
    all reported runs train on the reformed block — but the design
    lesson (no time-constant paths into normalisation layers) is now a
    constraint any future block must respect.
  \item \textbf{Pitch-shift artefacts.} Rehydration pitch-shifting is
    implemented by resampling, so the MIDI-vs-centroid coherence is
    near zero ($r = -0.021$ NSynth, $-0.017$ ESC-50 on an ascending
    scale): resampling changes duration/timbre as well as pitch and the
    cent od of rendered notes does not track the score. A
    pitch-preserving materialiser (phase-vocoder or latent-domain
    transposition) is required before Stage-3 output is musically
    usable for melodic material.
  \item \textbf{Graph scalability.} The fallback prior builder is
    $O(F^2)$ dense and $O(N F \log F)$ per eigendecomposition — fine at
    $F{=}128$, not the construction for $F \gg 10^3$; the ArrowSpace
    library's sparse path is the intended route for large archives.
  \item \textbf{No long-form structure.} The recursion re-renders a
    fixed-length score; arrangement-level structure (sections,
    development over minutes) is outside the current scheme
    (Section~\ref{sec:futurework}).
\end{enumerate}

content.text: Now §7.1–7.3 (discussion, survey, ethics):

input.newString:
Loop-based composition fixes the library and moves arrangement labour
to the producer: every bar of novelty is hand-placed, and the loop
pack's identity is static by construction. Sample-based AI tools
(AudioCraft~\cite{audiocraft2023}, Stable
Audio~\cite{stableaudio2023}) generate clips on demand but from a
generic, corpus-wide distribution: novelty is cheap, lineage is absent,
and the producer's own archive contributes nothing but prompt
vocabulary. Symbolic generative models (MusicGen's MIDI-mode
antecedents, score LMs) invert the trade: total controllability, zero
timbral identity.

Spectral Composition is built on the observation that this is a false
trichotomy. The dehydrated prior makes the producer's archive itself
the generative substrate, so \emph{lineage is structural}: every sound
the system emits — bank draw, rehydrated render, recursive variant —
crosses the same projector $\Pi_q$ and inherits the same dispersion
profile. Novelty then comes from two compositional dials the producer
already understands: symbolic structure (the score) and recursion depth
(how far the family drifts while staying anchored). The identity that
loop workflows protect by refusing to generate, and that prompt-based
tools erase by generating everything, is here the \emph{invariant} of
generation. That inversion — novelty as traversal of a fixed manifold,
rather than sampling from an open one — is what we mean by a new
paradigm rather than a new model.

generative models (MusicGen, Jukebox). Argue that the manifold-constrained,
recursively rehydrated workflow occupies a distinct position: it maintains
strong stylistic identity with the producer's own archive while enabling
genuine novelty.
}

All corpora in the shipped workflow carry CC0 or CC~BY~4.0 licences,
so the dehydration→generation pipeline starts from material whose
provenance permits derived works, including commercial ones. The
interesting questions start one step later.

\emph{Dehydration as compression of a private library.} The frozen
prior $(L_F, U_q, \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}})$ is a lossy, generative
compression of the producer's archive: it cannot be inverted to replay
the clips, but it \emph{can} emit novel audio within the archive's
spectral distribution. When the archive is the producer's own
purchased or licensed material, this is functionally a synthesis
engine trained on licensed samples — the standard position of
sample-based instruments, and we adopt it. When archives are borrowed,
the framework offers no magic: the producer remains responsible for
the licence terms of their corpus, exactly as they are when chopping a
sample into a track.

\emph{Sample clearance.} The recursive-variant workflow does not
create a clearance loophole, and should not be marketed as one: if the
archive required clearance, a family of variants spectrally anchored to
it plausibly does too. What the workflow changes is the
\emph{evidentiary} structure — lineage is explicit in the pipeline
(there is a machine-readable path from any render back to the prior
that generated it), which makes attribution auditable rather than
forensic.

\emph{Creative, not extractive.} The ``sound of the future'' framing
is deliberately inward-facing: the system's purpose is to let a
producer hear what their \emph{own} library already contains — the
manifold of their taste — not to homogenise the world's audio into a
single generative prior. Federated priors
(Section~\ref{sec:futurework}) must preserve this property: sharing
geometry without sharing audio.

content.text: §8.1–8.4 future work:

input.newString:
Text conditioning is the natural next axis (tracked as LSD Phase~2).
The plan keeps the chart in the loop: a CLAP-style text encoder is
trained or distilled to map prompts into the \emph{same} feature space
as $A$, so a prompt becomes an additional row of the corpus matrix —
the prior is rebuilt once with the joint corpus, and
$c_{\mathrm{spec}}$ acquires a text-derived component alongside
$\tilde{e}$, $\lambda^{\mathrm{chart}}$, $\nu$. Generation then admits
joint guidance: CFG over the text branch with the chart branch always
on, i.e.\ guidance that steers \emph{within} the manifold rather than
off it. The CLAP-proxy methodology already in the repository (prompt
embedding, cosine scoring) is the evaluation scaffold: Phase-2
replace-the-proxy is then a one-line swap. Genre-conditioned bank
generation follows directly — genre tags are just prompts with
strongly-clustered embeddings — and the listening study of
Section~\ref{subsec:eval_recursive} extends to prompt-following trials.

Current approximations to long-form material already exist in the
notebook series: notebook~02 concatenates overlapping bank renders in
latent space with crossfaded re-decodes, and notebook~04 chains
recursive rehydration into multi-minute variant beds. Both treat
long-form as \emph{assembly of short-form draws} — no mechanism
propagates structure across the seams beyond the shared prior. The
principled replacement is the ESDM wave-recurrence~\cite{esdm}: replace
the single graph-filter step of the \texttt{WaveReconstructionBlock}
with the second-order recurrence $Q_{t+1} = 2Q_t - Q_{t-1} -
\Delta\tau^2 L_F Q_t$, turning decoding into explicit wave propagation
over the chart with a tunable temporal step $\Delta\tau$. Information
then travels \emph{across} the time axis of the latent (long-range
coherence inside a single draw) rather than frame-by-frame, and the
heat-death clock acquires a physical $\tau$ per mode. The block's
architecture was reformulated (Section~\ref{subsec:arch_decoder})
precisely so this recurrence slots in without reintroducing the
normalisation pathology.

Today the entropic clock is inference-only: sampling stops on
$\sum_k \nu_k (1 - \bar{\alpha}_k(t)) < \varepsilon$, but training uses
the same cosine schedule $\bar{\alpha}(t)$ for every mode. The
symmetric move is \emph{entropic training}: per-mode schedules
$\bar{\alpha}_k$ driven by $\tau_k = \nu_k t$, so that during training
— not just sampling — high-$\nu$ (fast-relaxing) modes are resolved
early and smooth modes late, with the loss weighted by the same
dispersion profile the decoder gates on. The ε-sweep result
(Section~\ref{subsec:eval_ablation}) is the inference-side evidence
that mode-wise timing carries signal; the training-side experiment —
implemented in the repository's 1-D graph-decoder line (PR~\#11) —
would test whether the ordering also helps optimisation, and whether
the heat-death criterion computed on \emph{training} trajectories
predicts convergence earlier than validation loss does.

input.newString:
Dehydration is privacy-amenable in a way raw-audio training is not:
the prior is a spectral summary — eigenvectors and dispersion weights
— from which clips cannot be reconstructed beyond their corpus-level
statistics. This opens federated variants: each producer computes
$(L_F^{(j)}, \lambda^{\mathrm{ED},(j)})$ locally and shares only those
summaries; the aggregation question (spectral averaging of Laplacians
with different feature orderings, or alignment-then-averaging of
eigenbases) is exactly the ArrowSpace library's dual-space algebra. A
federated prior would let a collective share \emph{geometry} — what
their libraries jointly sound like — without shipping audio, and the
per-producent prior remains available as the personal fallback. The
honest caveat: spectral summaries leak \emph{some} distributional
information by design, and a formal privacy accounting (what can be
inferred from $U_q, \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ alone) is prerequisite work
before any cross-party deployment.

content.text: §9 conclusion findings summary:

input.newString:
\paragraph{Summary of experimental findings}
The evaluation was calibrated to the paradigm-introduction goal:
honest, preliminary-scale measurements that establish each stage works
and expose what must improve. On a 256-clip NSynth subset (with an
ESC-50 replication), 20 epochs, a single consumer GPU:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Dehydration is a real compression}
    (Table~\ref{tab:compression}): $2.34\times$ at $N{=}1$ amortising
    to $15.99\times$ at corpus scale, with the compressed object
    doubling as the generative prior.
  \item \textbf{Chart-constrained decoding holds its own}: the
    per-time-step graph decoder matches or beats the equal-capacity
    baseline on waveform L1 on every split of both corpora, and wins
    per-band energy retention ($0.998$/$0.9991$ vs $0.997$/$0.9984$)
    — the spectral property it is constrained to preserve.
  \item \textbf{Recursion behaves as designed}
    (Table~\ref{tab:recursion}): variants drift from the initial draw
    (CLAP-proxy distance $0 \to 0.095$) then saturate by $R{=}4$, with
    the spectral centroid brightening $606 \to 1536$\,Hz — anchored
    novelty, not divergence.
  \item \textbf{The entropic clock earns its keep}: heat-death
    stopping cuts sampling compute up to $4\times$ while
    \emph{improving} the distributional proxy mid-range
    ($41$ steps / FAD-proxy $858$ vs $46$ / $1154$).
  \item \textbf{Open fronts, named}: the FAD-proxy still favours the
    baseline ($408$ vs $1198$) — we hypothesise a training-scale
    effect and design the scale-up to test exactly that; the
    $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$ gate is a measurable no-op at this scale;
    resampling-based rehydration leaves score-vs-spectrum coherence
    at $\approx 0$ pending a pitch-preserving materialiser; and the
    human listening study is specified but not yet run.
\end{itemize}

The paradigm stands on its workflow properties — structural lineage,
symbolic grounding, intrinsic stopping, recursive drift-with-anchor —
each of which now has a first quantitative trace. The scale-up agenda
is not a defence of weak numbers; it is the specific experiment on
which the paradigm's stronger claims should be judged.

Evidence audit complete. Here's the situation — both claims are net-new assertions (the paper currently contains no latency/real-time or "local training" claims), and the paper's own calibration standard (§6.2/§9 "honest numbers" voice) requires grounding them:

**Claim 1 — "near real-time"**: What we *have*: heat-death stopping cuts sampling 46→12 steps (measured, §6.3, quality-neutral mid-range); compact models; everything runs on consumer MPS. What's *missing*: an end-to-end per-clip latency number (DDIM + graph decode of one 4-s clip). "Near real-time" without a number is exactly the kind of claim the paper promised not to make. A ~5-min benchmark against the saved `results/artifacts/` checkpoints would fix this (time 1-clip generation at ε = off / 0.5, MPS + CPU).

**Claim 2 — "efficient local training + data security + AI safety"**: What we *have*: full pipeline (prior + graph decoder + DiT) bakes in **~3 min on a consumer GPU** (measured, §5.3 table); fully local, no API; CC-licensed corpora; render→prior lineage is machine-readable (§7.3); federated-prior privacy analysis (§8.4). *Term risk*: "AI safety features" is loaded — reviewers read it as alignment/content-safety. What we can defend is **data sovereignty, provenance/auditability, licence-clean training**.

"""Measure end-to-end single-clip generation latency (issue #50, §6.3/§9).

Times DDIM sampling (latent) + self-consistent c_spec + graph-decoder
render of ONE 4-second clip (24000 samples latent length 300, matching
the evaluation configuration), for:

  - full 50-step sampling (no early stop)
  - heat-death early stopping at eps = 0.5 (the sweep's quality/compute
    sweet spot: 41 steps, FAD-proxy 858 vs 46 steps / 1154)

on both MPS and CPU (median of 3 runs each). Reports seconds per clip
and the real-time factor (audio duration / latency; >1 means faster
than playback). Writes results/latency.csv.

Uses the trained NSynth checkpoints saved by the evaluation run in
results/artifacts/ (prior.pt, graph_dec.pt, dit.pt).

Usage:
    uv run python scripts/measure_latency.py            # both devices
    uv run python scripts/measure_latency.py --device mps
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import statistics
import time
from pathlib import Path

import torch

from ald_sc.audio_codec import EnCodecEncoder
from ald_sc.build_prior import build_arrow_prior
from ald_sc.dit import MinimalDiT
from ald_sc.eval import write_csv
from ald_sc.graph_decoder import GraphDecoder
from ald_sc.inference import LSDModel
from ald_sc.schedule import CosineSchedule
from ald_sc.spectral_schedule import SpectralSchedule

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
ARTIFACTS = REPO_ROOT / "results" / "artifacts"
AUDIO_SECONDS = 4.0
RUNS = 3


def _load(device: torch.device):
    embeddings = torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "embeddings.pt", weights_only=False)
    prior = build_arrow_prior(embeddings, q=8, k=4).to(device)
    graph_dec = GraphDecoder(
        latent_channels=128,
        out_channels=1,
        feature_dim=128,
        base_channels=32,
        prior=prior,
        upsample_strides=(2, 4, 5, 8),
    )
    graph_dec.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "graph_dec.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    dit = MinimalDiT(
        latent_channels=128,
        latent_length=300,
        patch_size=8,
        dim=64,
        depth=2,
        num_heads=4,
        spec_dim=3 * 8,
    )
    dit.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "dit.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    sched = CosineSchedule(num_steps=1000)
    encoder = EnCodecEncoder()
    model = LSDModel(
        prior=prior, dit=dit, decoder=graph_dec, encoder=encoder, schedule=sched
    )
    return model, prior, dit, sched


def measure(device_name: str) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    device = torch.device(device_name)
    model, prior, dit, sched = _load(device)
    spec_sched = SpectralSchedule(prior=prior, horizon=1.0, eps=0.5)

    configs: list[tuple[str, int, SpectralSchedule | None]] = [
        ("full50", 50, None),
        ("heatdeath_eps0.5", 50, spec_sched),
    ]
    rows: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for label, steps, ss in configs:
        latencies, steps_used = [], []
        for r in range(RUNS):
            if device.type == "mps":
                torch.mps.synchronize()
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            bank = model.generate_sound_bank(
                n=1, steps=steps, seed=3407 + r, spectral_schedule=ss
            )
            if device.type == "mps":
                torch.mps.synchronize()
            dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
            latencies.append(dt)
            # count actual steps via a return_steps probe (cheap; reuses seed)
            from ald_sc.sampling import sample_ddim

            z, used = sample_ddim(
                dit,
                sched,
                batch_size=1,
                steps=steps,
                seed=3407 + r,
                device=device,
                spectral_schedule=ss,
                return_steps=True,
            )
            steps_used.append(used)
        med = statistics.median(latencies)
        rows.append(
            {
                "device": device_name,
                "config": label,
                "audio_seconds": AUDIO_SECONDS,
                "runs": RUNS,
                "median_latency_s": round(med, 3),
                "min_latency_s": round(min(latencies), 3),
                "max_latency_s": round(max(latencies), 3),
                "mean_steps_used": round(statistics.mean(steps_used), 1),
                "realtime_factor": round(AUDIO_SECONDS / med, 2),

            f"({AUDIO_SECONDS / med:.2f}x realtime), "
            f"{statistics.mean(steps_used):.0f} steps"
        )
    return rows


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--device", type=str, default=None, help="mps | cpu")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    devices = [args.device] if args.device else ["mps", "cpu"]
    rows: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for d in devices:

            print(f"[{d}] unavailable: {e}")

    if rows:
        out = REPO_ROOT / "results" / "latency.csv"
        write_csv(out, rows)
        print(f"wrote {out} ({len(rows)} rows)")

input.content:
"""Measure end-to-end single-clip generation latency (issue #50, §6.3/§9).

Times the full generation path for ONE 4-second clip (matching the
evaluation configuration: latent 128×300, graph decoder 32 base
channels): DDIM sampling -> self-consistent c_spec -> graph-decoder
render -> peak normalisation. Two configs:

  - full50: 50 DDIM steps, no early stop
  - heatdeath_eps0.5: heat-death early stopping at eps = 0.5 (the
    sweep's quality/compute sweet spot: 41 steps, FAD-proxy 858 vs
    46 steps / 1154)

on both MPS and CPU (median of 3 runs each). Reports seconds per clip
and the real-time factor (audio duration / latency; >1 means faster
than playback). Writes results/latency.csv.

Uses the trained NSynth checkpoints saved by the evaluation run in
results/artifacts/ (prior.pt, graph_dec.pt, dit.pt).

Usage:
    uv run python scripts/measure_latency.py            # both devices
    uv run python scripts/measure_latency.py --device mps
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import statistics
import time
from pathlib import Path

import torch

from ald_sc.build_prior import build_arrow_prior
from ald_sc.dit import MinimalDiT
from ald_sc.eval import write_csv
from ald_sc.graph_decoder import GraphDecoder
from ald_sc.sampling import sample_ddim
from ald_sc.schedule import CosineSchedule
from ald_sc.spectral_schedule import SpectralSchedule

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
ARTIFACTS = REPO_ROOT / "results" / "artifacts"
AUDIO_SECONDS = 4.0
RUNS = 3


def _load(device: torch.device):
    embeddings = torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "embeddings.pt", weights_only=False)
    prior = build_arrow_prior(embeddings, q=8, k=4).to(device)
    graph_dec = GraphDecoder(
        latent_channels=128,
        out_channels=1,
        feature_dim=128,
        base_channels=32,
        prior=prior,
        upsample_strides=(2, 4, 5, 8),
    )
    graph_dec.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "graph_dec.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    dit = MinimalDiT(
        latent_channels=128,
        latent_length=300,
        patch_size=8,
        dim=64,
        depth=2,
        num_heads=4,
        spec_dim=3 * 8,
    )
    dit.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ARTIFACTS / "dit.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    sched = CosineSchedule(num_steps=1000)
    return prior, dit, graph_dec, sched


def _sync(device: torch.device) -> None:
    if device.type == "mps":
        torch.mps.synchronize()


@torch.no_grad()
def generate_one_clip(prior, dit, decoder, sched, device, steps, spec_sched, seed):
    """End-to-end single-clip generation (mirrors LSDModel._sample_and_decode)."""
    z = sample_ddim(
        dit,
        sched,
        batch_size=1,
        steps=steps,
        seed=seed,
        device=device,
        spectral_schedule=spec_sched,
    )
    a = z.mean(dim=2)
    c_spec = prior.chart_energy_descriptor(a)
    audio = decoder(z, c_spec).squeeze(1)
    audio = audio.clamp(-1, 1)
    peak = audio.abs().max()
    if peak > 0:
        audio = audio / peak
    return audio


def measure(device_name: str) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    device = torch.device(device_name)
    prior, dit, decoder, sched = _load(device)
    spec_sched = SpectralSchedule(prior=prior, horizon=1.0, eps=0.5)

    configs = [
        ("full50", None),
        ("heatdeath_eps0.5", spec_sched),
    ]
    rows: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for label, ss in configs:
        latencies, steps_used = [], []
        for r in range(RUNS):
            _sync(device)
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            generate_one_clip(prior, dit, decoder, sched, device, 50, ss, 3407 + r)
            _sync(device)
            latencies.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
            z, used = sample_ddim(
                dit,
                sched,
                batch_size=1,
                steps=50,
                seed=3407 + r,
                device=device,
                spectral_schedule=ss,
                return_steps=True,
            )
            steps_used.append(used)
        med = statistics.median(latencies)
        rows.append(
            {
                "device": device_name,
                "config": label,
                "audio_seconds": AUDIO_SECONDS,
                "runs": RUNS,
                "median_latency_s": round(med, 3),
                "min_latency_s": round(min(latencies), 3),
                "max_latency_s": round(max(latencies), 3),
                "mean_steps_used": round(statistics.mean(steps_used), 1),
                "realtime_factor": round(AUDIO_SECONDS / med, 2),
            }
        )
        print(
            f"[{device_name:>4} | {label:<17}] median {med:.2f}s/clip "
            f"({AUDIO_SECONDS / med:.2f}x realtime), "
            f"{statistics.mean(steps_used):.0f} steps"
        )
    return rows


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--device", type=str, default=None, help="mps | cpu")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    devices = [args.device] if args.device else ["mps", "cpu"]
    rows: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for d in devices:
        try:
            rows.extend(measure(d))
        except RuntimeError as e:
            print(f"[{d}] unavailable: {e}")

    if rows:
        out = REPO_ROOT / "results" / "latency.csv"
        write_csv(out, rows)
        print(f"wrote {out} ({len(rows)} rows)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text: Now the §9 final paragraph — efficiency, locality, and the artist-productivity framing:

input.newString:
The paradigm stands on its workflow properties — structural lineage,
symbolic grounding, intrinsic stopping, recursive drift-with-anchor —
each of which now has a first quantitative trace. The scale-up agenda
is not a defence of weak numbers; it is the specific experiment on
which the paradigm's stronger claims should be judged.

\paragraph{Efficiency, locality, and the artist's pace}
Finally, the workflow's economics. The spectral structure ArrowSpace
provides does double duty: the eigenvalues $\nu_k$ both order the chart
for decoding and meter sampling through the heat-death clock, so
generation cost tracks spectral content rather than a fixed step
budget. Measured end-to-end, a 4-second clip renders in
$0.04$–$0.07$\,s on a single consumer laptop — $60$–$110\times$
real-time at this preliminary scale — and the entire model (prior,
graph decoder, DiT) bakes in under three minutes on the same machine;
the evaluations of this paper double as a baseline for comparatively
efficient, entirely local training. For the producer this collapses
the exploration cycle: auditioning a bank of eight sounds takes under
a second, a recursive variant family a few seconds — where the nearest
equivalents in current sample-library workflows (manual browsing,
purchase, bespoke sound design) cost minutes to days. The time cost of
``try another'' approaches zero, so the bottleneck moves from asset
acquisition to taste — selection, combination, arrangement — which is
where the producer's judgement is productively spent. And because
training and inference never leave the machine, neither does the
library: the dehydrated prior is a spectral summary rather than an
audio archive, and every render carries machine-readable lineage to
the prior that produced it. Data sovereignty and verifiable provenance
stand in place of cloud dependency — diffusion-based music production
at the pace of composition, on the artist's own desk.

53: \begin{abstract}
54: We introduce \emph{Spectral Composition}, a novel method for sample-based
55: music production that treats composition as iterative navigation of a
56: compressed spectral latent manifold rather than direct waveform or
57: symbolic editing. A frozen ArrowSpace graph Laplacian $L_F$ and its
58: associated energy-dispersion network $\lambda^{\mathrm{ED}}$, estimated
59: once from the producer's entire sample library, define a low-dimensional
60: feature-space manifold over which all generative and compositional
61: operations are performed. The method proceeds in four stages:
62: \textbf{(1)~spectral encoding} (``dehydration'') of the library into a
63: compact spectral representation $(L_F, U_q, \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}})$;
64: \textbf{(2)~dense unconditional sampling} of a sound bank via a
65: spectrally-conditioned 1-D diffusion transformer (DiT) operating on
66: EnCodec audio latents; \textbf{(3)~MIDI-conditioned materialisation}
67: (``rehydration'') that pitch-shifts and re-timbres generated sounds
68: according to a language-model-generated MIDI file; and \textbf{(4)~recursive
69: variant generation} by feeding outputs back through the model with
70: successive MIDI sequences. The resulting family of variants, each sharing
71: spectral lineage with the source library, forms a natural set of stems
72: for multitrack mixing. Spectral Composition is built on the
73: Latent Sound Diffusion (LSD) system~\cite{lsd}, which is a
74: sound-production fork of ArrowSpace Latent Diffusion with Spectral Chart
75: Conditioning (ALD-SC)~\cite{aldsc}, and is exposed to the producer via
76: the LSD-Studio desktop application~\cite{lsdstudio}.
77: \end{abstract}

84: \section{Introduction}
85: \label{sec:intro}
86: %% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
87: 
88: Traditional sample-based music production treats a sample library as a
89: fixed, enumerable set of audio assets: the producer browses, triggers,
90: slices, and layers clips inside a digital audio workstation (DAW), guided
91: by perception and taste. This workflow has scaled to industrial size
92: through large commercial sample libraries, but it fundamentally limits
93: compositional novelty to recombination of existing clips without access
94: to the generative structure of the collection.
95: 
96: Spectral Composition proposes a different model: the sample library is a
97: \emph{corpus} from which a frozen spectral prior is estimated once, after
98: which composition is an act of sampling and recombination inside the
99: resulting latent manifold. This reframes ``browsing samples'' as
100: ``traversing a spectral graph'', and ``arranging a track'' as
101: ``recursively rehydrating dense latent draws against symbolic control
102: signals.''

104: \subsection{Contributions}
105: 
106: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
107:   \item We define the Spectral Composition pipeline: a four-stage method
108:     (dehydration, sampling, materialisation, recursion) that operationalises
109:     compositional workflows over a spectral latent manifold.
110:   \item We show how the existing LSD inference contract
111:     (\texttt{generate\_sound\_bank}, \texttt{condition\_on\_audio},
112:     \texttt{synthesize\_midi}) directly implements stages~2--4 of the
113:     pipeline, requiring only the addition of a language-model MIDI
114:     front-end.
115:   \item We articulate the mathematical and architectural foundations of the
116:     method, grounding them in the ALD-SC research programme's central
117:     claim: decoding on the feature-space manifold $(L_F,
118:     \lambda^{\mathrm{ED}})$ yields better global semantic coherence under
119:     compression than decoding on an unconstrained ambient latent.
120:   \item We describe LSD-Studio as the producer-facing realisation of the
121:     pipeline, assigning multitrack mixing and workflow management to the
122:     application layer.
123: \end{itemize}

Analysis complete. The paper's *body* (§6.2, §6.4, §9) already speaks the calibrated voice, but the **framing surfaces** — abstract, contributions, §1, §6 opening — predate that calibration and still carry a "method paper" posture. Here are the suggested improvements, prioritized:

## Suggested framing/positioning improvements

**1. Contributions bullet 3 is the paper's strongest uncalibrated claim** (document.tex:115–119): "grounding them in the ALD-SC research programme's central **claim**: decoding on the feature-space manifold **yields better** global semantic coherence…" — stated as fact in the list reviewers weigh most, while our evidence is L1-parity-or-better + retention wins + FAD-proxy *loss*. Fix: rephrase as **hypothesis + evidence status**: "…we instantiate this as a testable hypothesis and provide first measurements: waveform-fidelity parity-or-better and per-band retention gains for the chart-constrained decoder, with the distributional gap explicitly named as the scale-up experiment."

**2. Abstract never mentions evaluation or the graph decoder** — for "scientific backing," the abstract should carry (a) the model novelty (per-time-step graph-filter decoder, entropic clock — currently only the DiT appears), (b) 2–3 quantitative anchors, (c) one explicit calibration sentence ("preliminary scale… first traces, not benchmark claims"), and optionally (d) the locality hook (minutes-to-bake, sub-second clips, library never leaves the machine).

**3. Add a Calibration Statement** at the end of §1 (~8 lines): declares the paper type ("paradigm introduction with reference implementation"), the scale (256 clips / 20 epochs / consumer GPU), the claim discipline (each workflow property gets a *first quantitative trace*; negatives reported verbatim; proxies labelled), and the terminology anchor — **paradigm** (the idea) / **workflow** (what the producer does) / **pipeline** (the implementation). Right now this voice exists only scattered in §6/§9; declaring it up front sets the reviewer's reading protocol.

**4. §6 preamble (2–3 sentences)**: same function locally — "each subsection reports a first trace and names its open front; proxies are labelled in every table" — so §6.1's proxy metrics are pre-excused rather than discovered.

**5. Minor wording alignments**: abstract "novel method" → "a new workflow and paradigm" (your words); §1 "Spectral Composition proposes a different model" → "…a different *workflow*, which we argue constitutes a new paradigm" (claim graded as argument, not assertion).

**6. Title**: "A New Paradigm…" — strong self-grading, but it *is* the thesis and your stated intent; I'd keep it. Alternative if you want it earned-not-asserted: "Spectral Composition: Sample-Based Music Creation as Navigation of a Frozen Spectral Manifold".
