# LSD Studio

> Latent Sound Diffusion desktop app — Rust + iced frontend, Python generation workers.

## Quick start

### Prerequisites

| Tool | Min version | Install |
|---|---|---|
| `rustup` | stable | https://rustup.rs |
| `uv` | 0.4+ | https://docs.astral.sh/uv |
| `git` | 2.40+ | system package manager |

### Bootstrap

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/tuned-org-uk/LSD-studio
cd LSD-studio
make setup
```

`make setup` will:
1. Initialise the `latent-sound-diffusion` submodule
2. Verify your Rust toolchain and add `clippy` + `rustfmt` components
3. Create a `.venv` and install Python worker dependencies via `uv`
4. Download the GeneralUser GS soundfont (~30 MB)

### Build

```bash
make build    # debug build
make release  # optimised, stripped binary → target/release/lsd-studio
```

### Run

```bash
RUST_LOG=warn,lsd_studio=debug cargo run  # debug build + run
cargo run --release                       # optimised binary + run
```

The app writes a log to `logs/app.log` (relative to the working directory) and
to stderr. The default filter is `warn,lsd_studio=info`. Override it with the
standard `RUST_LOG` env var:

```bash
RUST_LOG=info cargo run                 # app info + dependency warnings
RUST_LOG=lsd_studio=debug cargo run     # verbose app logging
RUST_LOG=debug cargo run                # everything (noisy)
```

The first launch scans bundled samples and prompts to "bake" (train) the base
LSD model if the cached checkpoints are missing or stale. Baking runs the
`latent-sound-diffusion` trainer via `uv run python python/lsd_worker.py
--base-train ...` and streams progress to the startup screen.

LSD Studio ships with support for several commercially-licensed audio datasets.
Datasets are **not** bundled in the repository; they are downloaded on demand.

You can adjust the size and have multiple portions in different directories under

All datasets in `sound-archive/manifest.json` carry **CC0** or **CC BY 4.0** licenses,

# AGENTS.md — LSD Studio Development Guide

This file is the authoritative reference for AI agents and human contributors developing this repository.
Read it in full before making any changes. All decisions in code review trace back to these principles.

> **Skills:** Three opencode skills are installed locally at `.opencode/skills/` and are invoked by name
> via the skill tool. Their trigger conditions and chaining order are defined in § 16 (Skill
> Orchestration). Read § 16 before starting any non-trivial work — it tells you which skill to load
> and when. The per-domain adaptations of each skill live in § 12 (UI), § 14 (spec), and § 15
> (interview).
> Always use ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English

---

## 1. Project Overview

LSD Studio is a **Diffusion + MIDI Transformer desktop app** built in Rust (iced) with a Python backend.
It has two first-class generation modes that are architecturally equal:

| Backend | Generation method | Synthesis step |
|---|---|---|
| **LSD** (Latent Sound Diffusion) | Diffusion model → `.wav` directly | None |
| **MIDI-GPT** | Transformer → `.mid` symbols → FluidSynth → `.wav` | Inside Python worker |

From the Rust side, both backends are identical after the IPC boundary: they both emit `sample_ready`
events pointing to `.wav` files. The audio engine, DSP pipeline, effect chain, waveform canvas and
mixer panel are shared and contain no backend-specific branching.

The desktop app runs in **Rust** using [iced 0.13](https://github.com/iced-rs/iced).
Generation and synthesis run in **Python 3.13+** worker processes managed by the Rust app via
stdio JSON-lines IPC. Python workers are invoked with `uv run python <worker>.py ...`.

## 1.1 MVP and Sound Producing Model (LSD) Characteristics

From the user's perspective, the objectives and actionables for models training are:
1. user has a library of samples (sound archive) they want to leverage (in data/)
2. LSD trains a model on these samples to explore novelty of sound and potentially integrate into a sound production pipeline
3. user should be able to leverage the model in different ways:
   A. the model at inference time should produce a set of "output sounds" that are used as a baseline and the producer can select and pick from
   B. user can pass existing sounds to model inference to generate novelty, variants, apply effects
   C. user can pass a MIDI file and synthetise the MIDI symbols leveraging the sounds generated by LSD
In this scenario, the model once trained shall be able to produce a set of "output sounds" as a baseline. These baseline output sounds can be used in mixing, or passed themselves back to the model for further generation, or concatenated and effects added to it (see notebooks in `latent-sound-diffusion` for version of the code with tag 0.5.0+).

> **Submodule tracking policy:** The `latent-sound-diffusion` git submodule (at
> `latent-sound-diffusion/`) **must be kept at the latest tag** upstream
> (`https://github.com/tuned-org-uk/latent-sound-diffusion`). When starting work
> on this repo, run `git -C latent-sound-diffusion fetch --tags origin && git -C
> latent-sound-diffusion checkout <latest-tag>`, then commit the new submodule
> pointer in the parent repo. New runtime deps the tag introduces must be added
> to `python/requirements.txt` (which mirrors
> `latent-sound-diffusion/pyproject.toml`). The current pinned tag is recorded in
> the submodule's `git describe --tags` output.
>
> **Tag-bump API audit (mandatory):** Every time the submodule is moved to a new
> tag, the agent **must** audit the public API surface exposed to this repo —
> the Python worker entry points (`sample_ddim`, `train_audio_diffusion`,
> `train_audio_decoder`, `build_arrow_prior`, the `ald_sc.*` classes the workers
> import), and the CLI args of the `scripts/*.py` entry points. New parameters,
> new functions, or changed signatures are opportunities to expose features in
> the desktop UI. For each new surface item the agent must decide: (a) wire it
> in this PR with a version-gated knob/control, or (b) document it as a
> follow-up in `docs/specs/`. Features that land in the UI must be gated by the
> active model's `lsd_tag` via `AppState::lsd_supports("vX.Y.Z")` so that older

## 3. Architecture Principles

### 3.1 Shared pipeline contract

Every process — regardless of backend — passes through exactly these stages in this order:

```
Worker spawn  →  JSON-lines IPC  →  ProcessRecord lifecycle
  →  .wav on disk  →  rodio Sink  →  ADSR envelope  →  fundsp effects  →  Mixer
```

- **No backend logic leaks past the IPC boundary.** The Rust audio engine receives `.wav` paths only.
- **`SampleReady { path, midi_path: Option<PathBuf> }`** is the handoff event. The audio engine
  uses `path` (`.wav`). `midi_path` is stored in `ProcessRecord::midi_sidecar` and surfaced
  only by the Export MIDI button on MIDI-GPT cards.
- **The synthesis step (`.mid → .wav`) lives entirely inside `midi_gpt_worker.py`.** FluidSynth is
  called there; by the time Rust sees `sample_ready`, a `.wav` is ready.

### 3.2 `ProcessBackend` is the only discriminant

```rust
pub enum ProcessBackend {
    LSD    { seed: u32, steps: u32, epochs: u32, temperature: f32 },
    MidiGpt { model_name: String, num_bars: u8, temperature: f32,
              top_p: f32, mask_k: u32, note_density: Option<u32>,
              polyphony: Option<u32>, track_type: MidiTrackType },
}
```

`match backend { ... }` is allowed **only** in:
- `src/python/bridge.rs` — to dispatch to the correct Python script
- `src/ui/process_card.rs` — to render the correct knob set and the Export button
- `src/state.rs` — `ProcessBackend::default_label()` helper

Anywhere else, a `match` on `ProcessBackend` is a design smell and must be refactored.

### 3.3 IPC protocol is the contract between Rust and Python

Both workers emit newline-delimited JSON to stdout. The schema is fixed:

```json
{ "type": "prior" }
{ "type": "progress",    "epoch": 3,   "loss": 0.142 }
{ "type": "synthesising" }
{ "type": "sample_ready", "path": "/tmp/.../sample_000.wav", "midi_path": null }
{ "type": "done" }
{ "type": "error",       "msg": "..." }
```

- `midi_path` is present and non-null only from `midi_gpt_worker.py`.
- `synthesising` is emitted only from `midi_gpt_worker.py`; it maps to `ProcessStatus::Synthesising`.
- `loss` may be `null` for MIDI-GPT progress events.
- The same schema is used by the startup baking phase (`lsd_worker.py --base-train`); it only
  emits `progress` and `done` (no `sample_ready`).
- **Do not add worker-specific fields to this schema.** If new information must cross the boundary,
  add a new `type` value and update `WorkerEvent` in `src/python/ipc.rs` accordingly.

### 3.4 `ProcessStatus` lifecycle

```rust
pub enum ProcessStatus {
    Pending,

# User Guide: Datasets and the Baking Phase

## What is the baking phase?

LSD Studio learns a small base model from a dataset of audio samples. This is
called **baking**. It runs once at startup, before the main UI appears.

When baking is complete, LSD Studio uses the baked model as a starting point
for new generations, so generations are faster and more consistent.

## Downloading datasets

Datasets are **not** bundled with the app — you download them yourself. The
baking phase always uses the `tiny-196` dataset (196 NSynth samples). Download
it with:

```bash
uv run python scripts/download_nsynth.py --n_samples 196 --destdir sound-archive/bundled/tiny-196 --source hf
```

You can download larger datasets for training in the Train panel:

```bash
# 4K samples
uv run python scripts/download_nsynth.py --n_samples 4000 --destdir sound-archive/bundled/small-4K --source hf

# 10K samples
uv run python scripts/download_nsynth.py --n_samples 10000 --destdir sound-archive/bundled/large-10K --source hf

# 50K samples
uv run python scripts/download_nsynth.py --n_samples 50000 --destdir sound-archive/bundled/large-50K --source hf
```

Each command creates a subdirectory under `sound-archive/bundled/` containing
the downloaded `.wav` files.

## Selecting a dataset for training

1. Open the **Train** tab.
2. The **dataset** dropdown lists all subdirectories found under
   `sound-archive/bundled/` (e.g. `tiny-196`, `small-4K`, `large-10K`).
3. Select the dataset you want to train on.
4. Press **Start training**.

The selection persists across restarts in `settings-train.json`. The baking
phase at startup always uses `tiny-196` regardless of the dropdown selection.

If `tiny-196` is missing at startup, the baking screen shows an error with the
download command to run.

## What kind of samples are in NSynth?

NSynth (Neural Synthesis) is a dataset of ~300K short monophonic single
musical notes across 1006 instruments, released by Google Magenta under
Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (Engel et al., 2017). The partial downloads
above take the first N `.wav` files from each split — a diverse, unstratified
subset suitable for training small models.

## Training settings

The training settings are stored in a JSON file in the system application
directory:

- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/lsd-studio/settings-train.json`
- Linux: `~/.local/share/lsd-studio/settings-train.json`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\lsd-studio\settings-train.json`

An example file:

```json
{
  "toy_mode": false,
  "epochs": 100,
  "steps": 32,
  "temperature": 0.8,
  "seed": 42,
  "learning_rate": 0.0001,
  "batch_size": 16,
  "loss_weighting": "snr",
  "grad_clip": 1.0,
  "dataset": "tiny-196"
}
```

- `toy_mode`: When `true`, uses a tiny, fast configuration for testing.
- `epochs`: How many times the model sees the entire dataset.
- `steps`: Diffusion sampling steps used during validation.
- `temperature`: Sampling temperature (higher = more varied, lower = more focused).
- `seed`: Random seed for reproducible results.
- `learning_rate`: Optimizer step size.
- `batch_size`: Number of samples per training step.
- `dataset`: Which dataset subdirectory under `sound-archive/bundled/` to train
  on (default: `tiny-196`).

Edit the file while LSD Studio is closed. Changes are read at the next startup.

Now I have the precise picture of the full workflow. Here is the analysis.

## Short answer: it is close, but not quite additive synthesis — it is better described as **latent-space spectral composition**.

***

## Technical definition

Additive synthesis in the strict DSP sense means constructing a waveform by summing sinusoidal partials — each with independent frequency, amplitude, and phase . LSD-studio's workflow does not do that. What it actually does across the three stages is:

1. **Train** — a VAE maps your custom audio archive into a latent space shaped by an ArrowSpace spectral prior; the DiT learns the latent manifold of that specific sound world 
2. **LSD Generate** — DDIM reverse diffusion samples new points from that manifold, decodes them through a graph decoder conditioned on a spectral chart (`c_spec`), and applies an ADSR envelope + fundsp effect chain (reverb, LP/HP, gain) to the output waveform 
3. **MIDI-GPT Materialise** — a language model generates MIDI note sequences (`MidiTrackType`: melodic / chordal / bass / drums), which are then rendered by pitch-shifting and time-scaling LSD bank sounds, overlap-added into a final mono mix

The **additive** quality you are sensing is real but operates at the **compositional layer**, not the signal layer: multiple independent `ProcessRecord` instances — each a diffusion generation with its own seed, temperature, and envelope — are mixed together through a shared master volume and mute/solo matrix . That is closer to **additive multi-track composition from latent samples** than to additive synthesis.

The more precise technical framing is: **latent diffusion-based spectral composition** — where "spectral" refers to the ArrowSpace prior's chart energy descriptor (`c_spec`) that shapes both training and generation, and "composition" refers to the multi-process mixing layer.

***

## Marketing definition

> **"A personalised sound engine that learns your music, then generates infinite variations of it — arranged into full tracks with AI-composed MIDI."**

Or, tighter for a tagline:

> **"Train on your sounds. Generate from your world. Compose with AI."**

The three-panel workflow (Train → LSD → MIDI-GPT) maps cleanly onto a three-word pitch because each stage has a distinct and intuitive user action: you *teach* it, it *invents*, you *arrange*. The word "additive" could appear in marketing copy honestly in the sense that each generated process *adds* a new layer to the mix — but claiming it as a synthesis method would be technically misleading and invite pushback from audio engineers.

## Context

During the issue #50/#51 session (2026-08-15) the experiment codebase took
priority and `main` was force-pushed with the session's history
(`e6443ea`), leaving two earlier commits unintegrated. They are preserved
locally on branch **`deferred/entropic-clock-0.7.0`** (tip `64abb6b`); this
issue tracks deciding whether and how to reintegrate them.

## What is deferred

- `1581d73` — `feat: promote SpectralSchedule to dynamic Barontini entropic
  clock (#41)`: adds `DynamicEntropicClock` (a drop-in `SpectralSchedule`
  subclass accumulating τ from actual entropy flow between denoising steps,
  with warm-up fallback to the frozen schedule); the three samplers call
  `clock.update(x)` when available before `is_heat_death()`;
  `sample_audio.py` gains `--entropic-clock/--clock-eps/--tau-warmup`;
  `test_dynamic_entropic_clock.py` (20 tests).
- `64abb6b` — version bump to **0.7.0** (current `main` is 0.6.0).

## Why it is not a clean merge

`main` has since changed the same surface (commit `19a2953`, issue #51):

1. **`is_heat_death` semantics flipped to the reverse process**: base class
   now stops on remaining dissipation `Σ ν_k (1 − ᾱ_k(t)) < ε` (monotone
   during denoising; the old forward metric fired at the *start* of
   sampling). `DynamicEntropicClock` was written against the **old**
   semantics — its heat-death criterion and warm-up fallback must be
   re-derived on the new one, and `tests/test_spectral_schedule.py`
   (updated criterion) must pass alongside the 20 clock tests.
2. **`sampling.py`/`inference.py` overlap**: `clock.update(x)` call sites vs
   the MPS-safety rewrites (`_resample_1d` CPU path, device-matched RNG in
   `condition_on_audio`).
3. **Paper consistency**: the Spectral Composition paper (§2.3, §6.3, §8.3)
   and the ε-sweep deliverables (`results/sweep_eps.csv`,
   `results/latency.csv`) were produced with the **frozen** clock. If the
   dynamic clock lands, the §8.3 future-work text should name it as the
   in-flight direction and the sweep should optionally be re-run with
   `--entropic-clock` for a frozen-vs-dynamic comparison.

## Checklist (if we integrate)

- [ ] `git merge deferred/entropic-clock-0.7.0`; keep frozen
      `SpectralSchedule` (with new semantics) as default, dynamic clock
      opt-in.
- [ ] Re-derive `DynamicEntropicClock.is_heat_death` on the reverse-process
      criterion; unit tests for both clocks against the new semantics.
- [ ] Verify `clock.update(x)` call sites survive the MPS-safety rewrites;
      MPS parity tests (`tests/test_device_parity.py`) green with the clock.
- [ ] Re-run the ε sweep (frozen vs dynamic) on MPS; update §6.3 numbers if
      they move materially; add one sentence to §8.3.
- [ ] Bump version to 0.7.0 (from `64abb6b`) as its own commit.
- [ ] Full `uv run pytest tests/ -q`, `ruff check/format`, `pdflatex` ×3.

## If we do not integrate

Close this issue with the rationale (e.g. dynamic clock superseded by the
reverse-process criterion + scale-up agenda); the branch can then be
deleted. Either way the branch must not be dropped before the decision is
recorded here.

+class DynamicEntropicClock(SpectralSchedule):
+    """Dynamic Barontini entropic clock (issue #41).
+
+    Promotes ``SpectralSchedule`` from a frozen-prior stub to a dynamic
+    accumulator that advances τ only when entropy actually flows between
+    spectral sectors during generation.
+
+    The clock measures per-step entropy change of the "bright sector"
+    (active spectral modes) from the running variance of the denoised latent,
+    and accumulates it into τ_n:
+
+        Δτ = |S_bright(t) - S_bright(t-1)|
+        τ_n += Δτ
+
+    The dynamic ᾱ(τ_n) schedule is:
+
+        ᾱ_k(τ_n) = cos²(π/2 · τ_n / τ_max_est)
+
+    where τ_max_est is estimated from a warm-up window (first ``tau_warmup``
+    steps). Steps where entropy flows rapidly advance the schedule faster;
+    plateau steps contribute negligibly.
+
+    At equilibrium (no entropy change), τ_n stalls — Barontini's key property.
+
+    This class is a drop-in ``SpectralSchedule`` subclass: the sampler's
+    ``spectral_schedule`` hook and ``is_heat_death()`` interface are unchanged.
+    The sampler calls ``update(x)`` at each step to feed the current latent
+    before checking ``is_heat_death(t)``.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    prior : ArrowSpacePrior
+        The frozen ArrowSpace prior whose eigenvalues ν_k drive the schedule.
+    eps : float
+        Heat-death threshold for the stopping criterion.
+    tau_warmup : int
+        Number of warm-up steps for τ_max estimation.
+    """
+
+    def __init__(
+        self,
+        prior: ArrowSpacePrior,
+        eps: float = 1e-3,
+        tau_warmup: int = 5,
+    ) -> None:
+        super().__init__(prior, horizon=1.0, eps=eps)
+        self.tau_warmup = tau_warmup
+        self.tau_n: float = 0.0
+        self.tau_max_est: float | None = None
+        self._warmup_deltas: list[float] = []
+        self._prev_s_bright: Tensor | None = None
+
+    def _spectral_entropy(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
+        """Compute the spectral entropy (variance proxy) of the latent.
+
+        The bright-sector entropy proxy is the running variance of the
+        denoised latent. This is a lightweight signal that tracks how much
+        the latent is changing between denoising steps.
+
+        Parameters
+        ----------
+        x : Tensor (B, C, L)
+            Current latent.
+
+        Returns
+        -------
+        Tensor (scalar)
+            Bright-sector entropy proxy.
+        """
+        return x.var()
+
+    def update(self, x: Tensor) -> None:
+        """Advance the dynamic clock by one step.
+
+        Measures the entropy change |ΔS_bright| from the previous latent
+        state and accumulates it into τ_n. During the warm-up window,
+        collects Δτ samples to estimate τ_max_est.
+
+        Parameters
+        ----------
+        x : Tensor (B, C, L)
+            Current latent state from the sampler.
+        """
+        s_bright = self._spectral_entropy(x)
+
+        if self._prev_s_bright is None:
+            delta_tau = s_bright.abs().item()
+        else:
+            delta_tau = (s_bright - self._prev_s_bright).abs().item()
+        self.tau_n += delta_tau
+
+        if self.tau_max_est is None and len(self._warmup_deltas) < self.tau_warmup:
+            self._warmup_deltas.append(delta_tau)
+            if len(self._warmup_deltas) == self.tau_warmup:
+                total = sum(self._warmup_deltas)
+                self.tau_max_est = max(total, 1e-8)
+
+        self._prev_s_bright = s_bright.detach()
+
+    def alpha_bar_k(self, t: Tensor) -> Tensor:
+        """Per-mode noise schedule indexed by dynamic τ_n.
+

+
+        Returns

+            Per-mode alpha_bar.
+        """

+            return super().alpha_bar_k(t)

+        return torch.cos(torch.tensor(ratio * (math.pi / 2.0))).pow(2) * torch.ones_like(self.nu)

+        """
+        if self.tau_max_est is None:
+            return False
+        return self.heat_death_metric(t).item() < self.eps
+
+    def conserved(self) -> Tensor:
+        """Entropy conservation diagnostic: |S_bright + S_dark - S_0|.
+
+        Analogous to Barontini's experimental result 2 (S_bright + S_dark ≈ S_0).
+        Serves as a sanity check that the bright/dark sector split is
+        well-calibrated.
+
+        Returns
+        -------
+        Tensor (scalar)
+            Conservation error. Near-zero means well-calibrated.
+        """
+        if self._prev_s_bright is None:
+            return torch.tensor(0.0)
+        s_bright = self._prev_s_bright
+        s_dark = self.nu.sum() - s_bright
+        s_0 = self.nu.sum() / 2
+        return (s_bright + s_dark - s_0).abs()

Study complete. Here's the full analysis and proposed plan.

## What issue #52's deferred work actually contains

**`1581d73` (39 files) decomposes into:**

| Part | Content | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantic core** | `DynamicEntropicClock` (~185 lines, pure file-end addition), 3× `hasattr`-guarded `clock.update(x)` hooks in the samplers, `--entropic-clock/--clock-eps/--tau-warmup` CLI flags, `__init__` export, 20 new tests | **Port** |
| **Churn (~90% of the diff)** | Import reordering, multi-line→one-line collapses, blank-line removals across ~34 src/test/script files — *predating* main's current formatting | **Drop** |
| `64abb6b` | pyproject 0.6.0 → 0.7.0 | **Port** |

## Key finding: the semantic conflict is *smaller than issue #52 assumed*

I audited the clock against main's flipped `is_heat_death` (reverse-process remaining dissipation):

1. `DynamicEntropicClock` **fully overrides** `heat_death_metric`/`is_heat_death` — the base-class flip doesn't touch its post-warm-up behavior; warm-up fallback only uses `super().alpha_bar_k` (unchanged).
2. Its criterion `Σν·ᾱ(τ_n)` is **monotone-decreasing during sampling** because τ_n only accumulates — it does *not* inherit the old frozen-metric degeneracy I fixed. The two clocks are conceptually aligned: frozen = remaining dissipation in external time; dynamic = remaining structure in accumulated entropic time. Only a docstring note is needed, no re-derivation.
3. Their `test_frozen_schedule_still_works` only asserts output shape → passes under new semantics. All 20 tests should survive as-is.

**Ecosystem constraint discovered:** LSD-studio's specs pin the submodule by tag — "bumping from v0.7.0 to v0.8.0", "v0.7.0 knobs" — i.e. LSD-studio **already assumes v0.7.0 = the entropic-clock release**. Upstream main currently lacks that tag, so LSD-studio's submodule pinning is broken against this repo. Reintegration + tag `v0.7.0` repairs it.

**Known first-version limitations** (document, don't block): entropy proxy is global `x.var()` (not per-sector); `alpha_bar_k` broadcasts one scalar ᾱ to all modes; `.item()` per step syncs devices.

## Proposed plan

1. **Merge** `deferred/entropic-clock-0.7.0` into main (preserves #41 provenance); resolve the ~6 churn conflicts preferring main's side (MPS fixes, current tests) while accepting the semantic additions — only real conflict: `inference.py` reformat vs the MPS `_resample_1d` fix
2. Add one docstring note: dynamic criterion is in accumulated-τ coordinates (vs base's external-time remaining dissipation)
3. Full verification: pytest (expect ~243), ruff, `test_device_parity`
4. Bump to 0.7.0 + **tag `v0.7.0`** (repairs LSD-studio pinning) + delete the deferred branch
5. Close #52 with the decision record; optional: quick frozen-vs-dynamic ε sweep on MPS (~10 min, sampling-only) + one §8.3 sentence in the paper

## Plan: evidence-gated evaluation of the DynamicEntropicClock (issue #52)

### Phase A — Controlled comparison (no changes to main)

**Setup** (experiment scripts in temp dir, main untouched — the deferred code is imported from a copy of the branch file, and a local ~40-line DDIM loop adds the `clock.update(x)` hook main's samplers lack):

- Same harness as `measure_latency.py`/`resweep_eps.py`: NSynth artifacts from `results/artifacts/`, MPS, 16 fixed seeds, 50-step budget, FAD-proxy vs test-set features, wall-clock, steps used
- **Control**: frozen `SpectralSchedule` (main semantics) at its measured best point (ε=0.5 → 41 steps / FAD-proxy 858) + no-stop baseline (49 / 1154)
- **Dynamic**: `DynamicEntropicClock` sweep — ε ∈ {1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0} at warmup=5, plus warmup ∈ {3, 10} at the best ε; also record τ_n trajectories (does τ stall / fire sensibly?)
- Output: `results/sweep_clock.csv` + summary table on issue #52

**Pre-registered success criteria** (decided before running, per the paper's calibration discipline):
- **Primary**: ≥15% fewer mean steps than the frozen best (≤35) at FAD-proxy within ~5% of 858, **or** FAD-proxy ≥10% better at comparable steps
- **Secondary**: materially lower step-count variance across seeds
- **Failure modes** that close #52 as not-integrated: clock never fires in 50 steps (τ_max over-estimated), fires indiscriminately, or FAD-proxy degrades

### Phase B — Conditional integration (only on demonstrated advantage)

- Merge `deferred/entropic-clock-0.7.0`, resolving churn conflicts preferring main (MPS fixes, current tests), accepting the semantic core (class + hooks + CLI flags + export + 20 tests)
- Docstring note: dynamic criterion lives in accumulated-τ coordinates (vs base's external-time remaining dissipation)
- **No version bump, no tag** — pyproject stays 0.6.0 (dropping `64abb6b`'s change), main only
- Full pytest (~243 expected), ruff, device-parity, then delete the deferred branch

### Phase C — Record (unconditional)

- §8.3 paper note with the comparison outcome *verbatim* (advantage → numbers + in-flight direction; no advantage → negative result stated, frozen clock stays default at this scale); recompile ×3
- Close or update issue #52 with the decision + evidence table; commit

One consequence to flag: without a v0.7.0 tag, LSD-studio's submodule pinning ("v0.7.0 = entropic clock") stays broken — acceptable per your "keep only in main" directive; I'll note it on #52 so it's a recorded tradeoff, not an oversight.

"""Issue #52 evidence gate: frozen vs dynamic entropic clock (Phase A).

Controlled comparison on the NSynth eval artifacts, main's code untouched:
- Control arms: no-stop; frozen SpectralSchedule (MAIN semantics) eps=0.5
  (the measured sweet spot) and eps=1.0 for context.
- Dynamic arms: DynamicEntropicClock (deferred 1581d73) eps x warmup grid.
- Local DDIM loop replicates src/ald_sc/sampling.py sample_ddim exactly,
  plus the clock.update(x) hook as wired in the deferred commit.

Pre-registered success criteria (decided before running):
  Primary A: mean steps <= 35 (>=15% below frozen best 41) with FAD-proxy
             <= 901 (within 5% of 858)
  Primary B: FAD-proxy <= 772 (>=10% better than 858) with mean steps <= 47
  Integration proceeds only if some dynamic arm meets A or B.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import importlib.util
import random
import statistics
import time
from pathlib import Path

import torch

from ald_sc.audio_codec import EnCodecEncoder
from ald_sc.build_prior import build_arrow_prior
from ald_sc.data import AudioFolderDataset, build_audio_dataloader
from ald_sc.dit import MinimalDiT
from ald_sc.eval import encodec_pooled_features, fad_score, split_files, write_csv
from ald_sc.graph_decoder import GraphDecoder
from ald_sc.sampling import _init_noise, _pairwise
from ald_sc.schedule import CosineSchedule
from ald_sc.spectral_schedule import SpectralSchedule

DEFERRED = (
    "/var/folders/jp/_9hztzgd13s81lhsr83dn6y00000gn/T/opencode/"
    "deferred_spectral_schedule.py"
)
SEED, N_GEN, BUDGET = 3407, 16, 50
ART = Path("results/artifacts")


def _load_deferred():
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("deferred_sched", DEFERRED)
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod.DynamicEntropicClock


@torch.no_grad()
def local_ddim(model, schedule, seed, device, clock, tau_log=None):
    """Exact replica of main's sample_ddim loop + clock.update hook."""
    gen = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
    sigmas = schedule.sample_sigmas(BUDGET).to(device)
    x = _init_noise(model, 1, device, gen)
    used = 0
    for sig, sig_prev in _pairwise(sigmas.tolist()):
        if clock is not None:
            if hasattr(clock, "update"):
                clock.update(x)
            t_frac = sig / schedule.num_steps
            if clock.is_heat_death(torch.tensor(t_frac, device=device)):
                break
        used += 1
        t = torch.full((1,), int(sig), device=device, dtype=torch.long)
        v = model(x, t)
        ab = schedule.alpha_bar[int(sig)]
        ab_prev = schedule.alpha_bar[int(sig_prev)]
        z0_pred = ab.sqrt() * x - (1 - ab).sqrt() * v
        x = ab_prev.sqrt() * z0_pred + (1 - ab_prev).sqrt() * v
        if tau_log is not None and hasattr(clock, "tau_n"):
            tau_log.append(clock.tau_n)
    return x, used


@torch.no_grad()
def decode_clip(dec, prior, z, device):
    a = z.mean(dim=2)
    c_spec = prior.chart_energy_descriptor(a)
    xh = dec(z, c_spec).clamp(-1, 1).squeeze(0)
    peak = xh.abs().max()
    if peak > 0:
        xh = xh / peak
    return xh.unsqueeze(0)


def main():
    DynamicEntropicClock = _load_deferred()
    device = torch.device("mps")
    random.seed(SEED)
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)

    # Artifacts (identical to resweep_eps.py / measure_latency.py)
    embeddings = torch.load(ART / "embeddings.pt", weights_only=False)
    prior = build_arrow_prior(embeddings, q=8, k=4).to(device)
    dec = GraphDecoder(
        latent_channels=128, out_channels=1, feature_dim=128, base_channels=32,
        prior=prior, upsample_strides=(2, 4, 5, 8),
    ).to(device).eval()
    dec.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ART / "graph_dec.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    dit = MinimalDiT(
        latent_channels=128, latent_length=300, patch_size=8, dim=64,
        depth=2, num_heads=4, spec_dim=24,
    ).to(device).eval()
    dit.load_state_dict(
        torch.load(ART / "dit.pt", weights_only=False, map_location="cpu")
    )
    sched = CosineSchedule(num_steps=1000)

    # Reference features from the held-out test split
    all_files = sorted(Path("data").glob("*.wav"))
    selected = random.Random(SEED).sample(all_files, 256)
    _, _, test_files = split_files(selected, 0.7, 0.15, seed=SEED)
    test_ds = AudioFolderDataset(root="data", audio_length=96000)
    test_ds.files = test_files
    test_loader = build_audio_dataloader(test_ds, batch_size=8, shuffle=False)
    encoder = EnCodecEncoder()
    ref_feats = encodec_pooled_features((b for b in test_loader), encoder, device)
    print(f"ref features: {tuple(ref_feats.shape)}")

    def make_clock(arm):
        if arm["clock"] == "none":
            return None
        if arm["clock"] == "frozen":
            return SpectralSchedule(prior=prior, horizon=1.0, eps=arm["eps"])
        return DynamicEntropicClock(
            prior=prior, eps=arm["eps"], tau_warmup=arm["warmup"]
        )

    arms = [
        {"arm": "nostop", "clock": "none", "eps": None, "warmup": None},
        {"arm": "frozen_eps0.5", "clock": "frozen", "eps": 0.5, "warmup": None},
        {"arm": "frozen_eps1.0", "clock": "frozen", "eps": 1.0, "warmup": None},
    ]
    for eps in (1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0):
        for wu in (3, 5, 10):
            arms.append(
                {"arm": f"dyn_eps{eps:g}_wu{wu}", "clock": "dyn",
                 "eps": eps, "warmup": wu}
            )

    rows = []
    tau_traj = None
    for arm in arms:
        steps_used, walls, taus, tmax = [], [], [], []
        clips = []
        for i in range(N_GEN):
            clock = make_clock(arm)  # fresh clock per generation
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            z, used = local_ddim(
                dit, sched, SEED + i, device, clock,
                tau_log=[] if (i == 0 and arm["clock"] == "dyn") else None,
            )
            if device.type == "mps":
                torch.mps.synchronize()
            walls.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
            steps_used.append(used)
            if hasattr(clock, "tau_n"):
                taus.append(clock.tau_n)
                tmax.append(clock.tau_max_est or float("nan"))
            if i == 0 and arm["clock"] == "dyn":
                tau_traj = (arm["arm"], getattr(clock, "_warmup_deltas", None))
            clips.append(decode_clip(dec, prior, z, device).cpu())
        gen_feats = encodec_pooled_features(clips, encoder, device)
        fad = fad_score(gen_feats, ref_feats.cpu())
        row = {
            "arm": arm["arm"],
            "clock": arm["clock"],
            "eps": arm["eps"] if arm["eps"] is not None else "",
            "warmup": arm["warmup"] if arm["warmup"] is not None else "",
            "mean_steps": statistics.mean(steps_used),
            "min_steps": min(steps_used),
            "max_steps": max(steps_used),
            "n_fired": sum(1 for s in steps_used if s < BUDGET - 1),
            "FAD": round(fad, 2),
            "mean_wall_s": round(statistics.median(walls), 3),
            "tau_final_mean": round(statistics.mean(taus), 4) if taus else "",
            "tau_max_est_mean": round(statistics.mean(tmax), 4) if tmax else "",
        }
        rows.append(row)
        print(
            f"[{row['arm']:>18}] steps {row['mean_steps']:5.1f} "
            f"({row['min_steps']}-{row['max_steps']}, fired {row['n_fired']}/16) "
            f"FAD {row['FAD']:8.2f} wall {row['mean_wall_s']:.3f}s "
            f"{'tau ' + str(row['tau_final_mean']) if taus else ''}"
        )

    out = Path("results/sweep_clock.csv")
    write_csv(out, rows)
    print(f"wrote {out}")

    # Pre-registered gate evaluation
    FROZEN_BEST_FAD, FROZEN_BEST_STEPS = 858.0, 41.0
    print("\n=== Pre-registered gate ===")
    met = False
    for r in rows:
        if r["clock"] != "dyn":
            continue
        a = r["mean_steps"] <= 35 and r["FAD"] <= FROZEN_BEST_FAD * 1.05
        b = r["FAD"] <= FROZEN_BEST_FAD * 0.9 and r["mean_steps"] <= 47
        if a or b:
            met = True
            print(f"  MET ({'A' if a else 'B'}): {r['arm']} "
                  f"steps={r['mean_steps']:.1f} FAD={r['FAD']}")
    if not met:
        print("  NOT MET by any dynamic arm")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

@torch.no_grad()
def refine_ddim(model, schedule, z_init, device, clock, start_frac):
    """DDIM from a partially-noised latent: start at sigma index ~= start_frac.

    Uses the exact update rule of src/ald_sc/sampling.py sample_ddim; the
    clock gates the stop via the same is_heat_death(t_frac) check, plus the
    deferred clock.update(x) hook when present.
    """
    sigmas = schedule.sample_sigmas(BUDGET).tolist()
    k0 = int((1.0 - start_frac) * (len(sigmas) - 1))
    x = z_init.to(device)
    used = 0
    for sig, sig_prev in zip(sigmas[k0:], sigmas[k0 + 1 :]):

            t_frac = sig / schedule.num_steps

        t = torch.full((x.shape[0],), int(sig), device=device, dtype=torch.long)

    # Pre-encode conditioning clips
    cond = []
    for batch in loader:
        x = (batch if isinstance(batch, torch.Tensor) else batch[0]).to(device)
        z, _, _ = encoder.encode(x, prior)
        cond.append((x, z))
    print(f"{len(cond)} conditioning clips encoded")

    def make_clock(kind, eps):
        if kind == "none":
            return None
        if kind == "frozen":
            return SpectralSchedule(prior=prior, horizon=1.0, eps=eps)
        return DynamicEntropicClock(prior=prior, eps=eps, tau_warmup=5)

    arms = [
        ("interp_only", "none", None, 0.0),
        ("refine_eps0.5", "frozen", 0.5, STRENGTH),
        ("refine_eps1.0", "frozen", 1.0, STRENGTH),
        ("refine_eps2.0", "frozen", 2.0, STRENGTH),
        ("refine_eps5.0", "frozen", 5.0, STRENGTH),
        ("refine_nostop", "none", None, STRENGTH),
        ("full_ddim", "none", None, 1.0),
        ("dyn_wu5", "dyn", 1e-3, STRENGTH),
    ]

    interp_rel = None
    print(
        f"{'arm':>16} {'diversity':>10} {'rel->src':>9} {'RMS':>6} "
        f"{'steps':>10}"
    )
    for name, kind, eps, start_frac in arms:
        divs, rels, rmss, steps_hist = [], [], [], []
        for ci, (x_src, z_cond) in enumerate(cond):
            clips, src_feat = [], None
            for i in range(N_VAR):
                gen = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(SEED + ci * 100 + i)
                noise = torch.randn_like(z_cond, generator=gen)
                z_init = (1 - STRENGTH) * z_cond + STRENGTH * noise
                clock = make_clock(kind, eps)
                if start_frac == 0.0:
                    z = z_init
                    used = 0
                else:
                    z, used = refine_ddim(dit, sched, z_init, device, clock,
                                          start_frac)
                steps_hist.append(used)
                clips.append(decode(dec, prior, z).cpu())
            feats = encodec_pooled_features(clips, encoder, device)
            unit = feats / feats.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-12)
            sim = unit @ unit.T
            iu = torch.triu_indices(N_VAR, N_VAR, offset=1)
            divs.append((1.0 - sim[iu[0], iu[1]]).mean().item())
            src = encodec_pooled_features([x_src], encoder, device)[0]
            src = src / src.norm().clamp(min=1e-12)
            rels.append((1.0 - unit @ src.to(unit.device)).mean().item())
            rmss.append(
                torch.cat([c.pow(2).mean().unsqueeze(0) for c in clips]).sqrt().mean().item()
            )
        d, r, m = statistics.mean(divs), statistics.mean(rels), statistics.mean(rmss)
        if name == "interp_only":
            interp_rel = r
        print(
            f"{name:>16} {d:10.5f} {r:9.5f} {m:6.3f} "
            f"{statistics.mean(steps_hist):5.1f} "
            f"({min(steps_hist)}-{max(steps_hist)})"
        )

    print("\nPre-registered gate: diversity >= 0.01, rel <= 2x interp, RMS >= 0.35")
    if interp_rel is not None:
        print(f"(interp_only relatedness reference = {interp_rel:.5f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text: Root cause found — and it's deeper than the clock: **init noise differs (6.07) but the DDIM output differs by only 1.2e-06**. The undertrained unconditional DiT *contracts every noise draw to essentially one point* (the model's v-prediction is near input-independent, so DDIM's x-dependence decays with ᾱ′). That's why banks/variants measure zero diversity — no stopping rule can dial diversity out of a contracted sampler. **Answer to your question: no — and the investigation found something more important.**

I tested the idea directly (clock-gated SDEdit refinement of Mode-B variants, pre-registered gate): diversity gain = zero at every ε. Then traced it to the root cause:

**The undertrained DiT contracts every noise draw to one point.** Measured: init-noise max|diff| **6.1 → 1.2e-6** after 49 DDIM steps. So `generate_sound_bank(n)` returns n near-identical clips, and *any* stopping rule — clock or otherwise — just moves the endpoint along a 1-dimensional contraction path. There's no output distribution to dial diversity from.

Two useful positives fell out:
- **Mode-B interpolations (which bypass the sampler) genuinely differ** — waveform pairwise L1 0.13–0.17 — but the pooled-EnCodec diversity metric is blind to it (~1e-4). So variants *do* vary audibly today; the metric, not the model, reports ~0.
- The scale-up hypothesis (FAD-proxy gap) now has a **measured mechanism**: input-dependence of v_θ.

Landed (`832bcad`, pushed; #52 addendum posted): paper corrected where the finding invalidated claims — §3.2 "many voices" flagged as design-target-not-demonstrated, §6.3 diagnosis fixed (was wrongly "dominated by the DDIM noise draw"), §6.2 FAD-proxy single-sample caveat, §9 open fronts name the mechanism.

Real levers for diversity: the scale-up itself, or sampler-bypassing variant modes (interpolation+decode, which already works) — with a waveform-level diversity metric either way.
so what is the use of DDIM

On the current checkpoint, DDIM's honest job description has shrunk to three things — one measured, one designed, one deferred:

1. **Manifold projector (works, degenerately)**: DDIM is the map from noise onto whatever manifold the DiT learned. Right now that's ~a single point, so it produces *the model's canonical sound* — the "house voice" of a bake. That's bank Mode A: coherent by construction, but n draws = 1 voice (the 6.1 → 1.2e-6 contraction).
2. **Carrier of the heat-death clock (works, and pays)**: the ε sweep is real — stopping at 41/50 steps improved the FAD-proxy (858 vs 1154) and cut compute. The clock rides on DDIM's trajectory; no sampler, no intrinsic stopping.
3. **Interface to the learned distribution (deferred)**: DDIM's *intended* use — spreading noise across the corpus latent distribution — exists in the architecture but not yet in this checkpoint. It activates when v_θ becomes input-dependent (scale-up), with zero pipeline changes.

What it is *not* doing today: diversity generation. That currently lives in the sampler-bypass path (Mode-B interpolation → decode, waveform L1 0.13–0.17) and in NOISE_INJECT at training time.

So the practical read for the product today: **DDIM = canonical-sound generator + compute dial; interpolation = the variety mechanism.** After the scale-up, the roles re-merge as designed.

\paragraph{Role of the sampler at preliminary scale}
The contraction measurement lets us state precisely what DDIM does and
does not contribute at this training scale. It \emph{is} the manifold
projector — the map from noise onto whatever the DiT learned — but
projecting onto a near-single-point manifold, so each bank draw yields
the model's canonical sound (the bake's ``house voice''), coherent by
construction. It is also the carrier of the heat-death clock, and that
function is already productive: the $\varepsilon$ sweep of
Section~\ref{subsec:eval_ablation} rides on the DDIM trajectory and
buys its compute/quality tradeoff there. What the sampler does
\emph{not} currently provide is spread across the corpus distribution —
that role is deferred until $v_\theta$ becomes input-dependent at
scale, requiring no pipeline change. Meanwhile variety in the workflow
comes from the sampler-bypassing paths: Mode-B latent interpolation
(Stage~3) and the \texttt{NOISE\_INJECT} training dial. At preliminary
scale the division of labour is therefore: DDIM for the canonical sound
and the stopping dial, interpolation for the variety; the scale-up
re-merges the two roles as designed.

content.text:
**Recommendation: CC BY 4.0** — the standard for scholarly works on Zenodo/arXiv:

- Maximises dissemination and citation (anyone can reuse/reprint with attribution — exactly what a paradigm-introduction paper wants), keeps your copyright, and is compatible with later journal/arXiv submission
- **CC BY-SA 4.0** instead, if you want derivatives (translations, adaptations) forced open
- **CC0** only if you want zero attribution requirements (not advisable for a credit-dependent academic work)
- Avoid **CC BY-NC** — it chokes dissemination and complicates any future publisher transfer

Two practical notes: (1) publish the paper as its own Zenodo record — don't bundle it with a repo archive, since Zenodo applies one license per record and the code should carry its own; (2) your GitHub repo currently has **no LICENSE file** (all rights reserved by default) — if you want the "reference implementation available" claim in §5.1 to be legally true, add a code license (MIT/Apache-2.0, or CC-BY-4.0-if-considered-research-artifact) as a separate decision.
